It is said in reply: We observe that this is merely a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) whose nature remains unexamined. Let your honor examine this: Is this worldly linguistic usage—characterized by engagement or withdrawal based on the thought "this does not exist somewhere"—due to (1) non-apprehension, (2) the apprehension of something else, or (3) the apprehension of its absence? If it were due to non-apprehension, people would not seek to know the absence of what is desired; they would desist from it simply because of non-apprehension, and they would engage in what is undesired simply because of non-apprehension. [Objection: This usage is based precisely on the non-apprehension of the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Reply: No, because there is no distinction. For the non-apprehension of those two [the desired and the undesired] is not differentiated. Furthermore, it is incorrect to hold that engagement and withdrawal are preceded by a lack of cognition (*apratyaya*).

[48,i] It is false that [actions] proceed or cease because of the cognition of another entity (*vastvantara*), for that consequence would follow even when the counter-entity (*pratiyogin*) exists. When a jar and a thorn are being perceived, activity and cessation are based precisely on that [cognition]. Well then, the reversal [of these] occurs due to the absence of that [cognition], not due to the presence of another entity; for at that time as well, the cognition of the means to what is desired or undesired remains present and is prior [to action].

[52,i] The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth.”

Therefore, neither based on another valid cognition (*pramiti*) nor based on an invalid cognition (*apramiti*) do we have the notions "the undesired does not exist" or "the desired does not exist," which lead to engagement or withdrawal; rather, these are based on the apprehension of absence (*abhāva*). What has been determined as the object of the cognition "it does not exist"? Has it not already been stated? What offense has been committed by the non-existence of the object, such that you should disregard it and claim that the object of this [cognition] is the absence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*)? The non-existence of the knowable is not itself a cognizable object (*prameya*). Let it be so, provided there is some specific reason for the distinction. Just as there is an illusion of darkness when light is not seen, there is an illusion of cognition regarding the absence of cognition, and an illusion of practical activity (*vyavahāra*) regarding the absence of practical activity.
No; for this would entail the same consequence as in states such as deep sleep, and because error is impossible regarding that which is not cognized, just as in deep sleep and similar states.
[54,i] But the perception of darkness is the perception of the shadow of the earth.
And the perception of the absence of light is not the same [as the perception of the presence of light].
Or let it be that [the object] is graspable by a means of valid cognition; however, "existence" is said to be its being present.
There is an absence of an object for an injunction when there is the exclusion of the past and so forth in the verbal [cognition].
The state of not being the object of another [cognition] does not occur when another means of valid cognition arises.

[58,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchants being pursued by the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi; seeing them, he addressed the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi with these words: "O Yakṣa, do not kill these five hundred merchants! Do not kill them! The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi replied to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "I have already made a vow to eat these five hundred merchants. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who has no faith in the Three Jewels, no faith in the Buddha, no faith in the Dharma, and no faith in the Saṅgha; eat first the one who does not observe the precepts, who is unvirtuous, and who acts contrary to the Dharma. The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "I do not know which among these five hundred merchants has no faith in the Three Jewels, no faith in the Buddha, no faith in the Dharma, and no faith in the Saṅgha; I do not know which does not observe the precepts, is unvirtuous, and acts contrary to the Dharma. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who does not practice the six perfections, who does not seek the path of the bodhisattvas, and who does not aspire to supreme perfect enlightenment. The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Among these five hundred merchants, I do not see anyone who does not practice the six perfections, who does not seek the path of the bodhisattvas, or who does not aspire to supreme perfect enlightenment. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who does not take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; who does not take up the training rules; who does not give gifts; who does not perform meritorious deeds; and who does not cultivate roots of goodness. The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Among these five hundred merchants, I do not see anyone who does not take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; who does not take up the training rules; who does not give gifts; who does not perform meritorious deeds; or who does not cultivate roots of goodness. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who does not recite the names of the Buddhas, who does not hear the Dharma, who does not attend upon the Saṅgha, who does not offer incense, flowers, necklaces, ointments, powders, garments, parasols, banners, or pennants to the Buddhas, and who does not honor the stūpas of the Tathāgatas. The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Among these five hundred merchants, I do not see anyone who does not recite the names of the Buddhas, who does not hear the Dharma, who does not attend upon the Saṅgha, who does not offer incense, flowers, necklaces, ointments, powders, garments, parasols, banners, or pennants to the Buddhas, or who does not honor the stūpas of the Tathāgatas. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who does not maintain the precepts of purity, who does not observe the eightfold fast, who does not abstain from meat, who does not abstain from alcohol, and who does not abstain from sexual intercourse. The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Among these five hundred merchants, I do not see anyone who does not maintain the precepts of purity, who does not observe the eightfold fast, who does not abstain from meat, who does not abstain from alcohol, or who does not abstain from sexual intercourse. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who does not believe in the law of cause and effect, who does not believe in the existence of future lives, who does not believe in the ripening of karma, and who does not believe in the existence of Arhats. The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Among these five hundred merchants, I do not see anyone who does not believe in the law of cause and effect, who does not believe in the existence of future lives, who does not believe in the ripening of karma, or who does not believe in the existence of Arhats. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who does not believe in the Bodhisattvas, who does not believe in the Mahāyāna, who does not believe in the Prajñāpāramitā, and who does not believe in the teachings of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Among these five hundred merchants, I do not see anyone who does not believe in the Bodhisattvas, who does not believe in the Mahāyāna, who does not believe in the Prajñāpāramitā, or who does not believe in the teachings of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who does not hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, who does not uphold it, who does not read it, who does not recite it, who does not explain it to others, and who does not copy it. The yakṣa Śūlapāṇi said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Among these five hundred merchants, I do not see anyone who does not hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, who does not uphold it, who does not read it, who does not recite it, who does not explain it to others, or who does not copy it. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. Therefore, I shall eat all of them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi: "If you must eat them, then eat first the one who does not practice compassion, who does not practice loving-kindness, who does not practice sympathetic joy, and who does not practice equ

If the injunction (*niyoga*) were not verbal (*aśābda*), then the meaning of the sentence "one who desires heaven" would be that it does not inform [the agent] that "it was not, is not, or will not be," nor that "he has been enjoined, is being enjoined, or will be enjoined. Thus, the qualification (*adhikāra*) would be well-defined. Now, if the negation of the past and so forth is not verbal, but rather—due to the injunction’s indifference toward them—is determined by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), then it is not the case that [the injunction] has no other object. For its state as such is determined by another means of knowledge; the distinction [of the injunction] from that [other means] lies in what is cognized through the word. This is like the fact that a mountain’s possession of fire is known through inference, even though it is already perceived. No, for when the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) is not apprehended, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) cannot be its object. Furthermore, if its state as such is understood from another source, then "one who desires heaven" is simply not under an injunction, since that [other source] is also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Or, if it is not so, then the statement regarding the distinction from the past and so forth is mere idle chatter. [Objection: The past and so forth are merely limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); and upon the cessation of an adjunct, there is neither the cessation nor the non-cognition of the possessor of the adjunct. [Reply: Let this be so in the case of other adjuncts, but here, the very definition [of the past etc. is absolute non-existence. Moreover, when the adjuncts of permanence and impermanence cease, the possessor of the adjunct cannot possibly exist. Perception (*pratyakṣa*), however, at the time of its initial arising, grasps only the form devoid of the adjuncts of difference; thus, there is no difference in the object [between perception and the injunction]. Since that which is not present lacks form, perception has the present as its object. [Reply: True, in reality (*vastutaḥ*), but not from the perspective of valid cognition (*pramititaḥ*). In reality, if there is a distinction from the present and so forth, there is a lack of self-nature (*nirātmakatva*); because it is absolutely unapprehended, the word’s independence from other means of knowledge does not arise from a difference in the object. This is a double-edged sword (*ubhayataspāśā*).

[60,i] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the southern regions, beheld five hundred merchants who were being pursued by a band of five hundred robbers. Seeing them, he manifested himself as a merchant leader and went before the robbers. He addressed them, saying: "O friends, do not harm these merchants; let us share our wealth together. When the robbers heard this, they were filled with joy and said: "O friend, you have spoken well. We shall indeed share our wealth together. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having manifested himself as a merchant leader, took all the goods from the merchants and gave them to the robbers. Having given them the goods, he then led the merchants away. When the robbers saw that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara had taken all the goods and was leading the merchants away, they became enraged and pursued him. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, seeing that the robbers were pursuing him, transformed himself into a great mountain. When the robbers saw the great mountain, they were terrified and fled. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara restored his original form and stood before the merchants. Seeing the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the merchants were filled with joy and said: "O Great Being, we take refuge in you. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: "O friends, do not fear. I am here to protect you. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having comforted the merchants, led them safely out of the southern regions. This is the first instance of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s power of skillful means. ||| [60,ii] ||| Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the eastern regions, beheld a woman named Bhadra who was afflicted by a severe illness. Seeing her, he manifested himself as a physician and went to her. He addressed her, saying: "O lady, what is your ailment? She replied: "I am suffering from a chronic fever. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having manifested himself as a physician, prescribed for her a medicinal herb called *amṛta*. She took the herb and her illness was immediately cured. When the woman Bhadra saw that her illness was cured, she was filled with joy and said: "O Great Physician, you have saved my life. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: "O lady, do not speak thus. I am here to relieve the suffering of all beings. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having comforted the woman Bhadra, taught her the Dharma. Having taught her the Dharma, he established her in the path of non-retrogression. This is the second instance of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s power of skillful means. ||| [60,iii] ||| Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the western regions, beheld a king named Śubhavyūha who was oppressed by a wicked minister. Seeing him, he manifested himself as a wise counselor and went before the king. He addressed the king, saying: "O Great King, do not trust this wicked minister; he intends to usurp your throne. The king replied: "O counselor, how can I know if he is wicked? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having manifested himself as a wise counselor, spoke a verse: "One who speaks harsh words without cause, who acts with malice toward the virtuous, and who seeks only his own gain at another's expense—such a person is known as wicked. When the king heard this verse, he understood that the minister was indeed wicked. Having understood this, he dismissed the minister. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having comforted the king, taught him the Dharma. Having taught him the Dharma, he established him in the practice of universal compassion. This is the third instance of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s power of skillful means. ||| [60,iv] ||| Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the northern regions, beheld a group of five hundred young women who were about to be sold into slavery. Seeing them, he manifested himself as a wealthy man and purchased them all. Having purchased them, he led them away. When the young women saw that they had been purchased by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they were filled with joy and said: "O Great Man, you have liberated us from bondage. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: "O sisters, do not speak thus. I am here to liberate all beings from the bonds of saṃsāra. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having comforted the young women, taught them the Dharma. Having taught them the Dharma, he established them in the stage of irreversible bodhisattvas. This is the fourth instance of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s power of skillful means. ||| [60,v] ||| Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the upper regions, beheld a great fire burning a city. Seeing it, he manifested himself as a rain-god and sent down a great rain. The rain extinguished the fire, and the city was saved. When the inhabitants of the city saw the fire extinguished, they were filled with joy and said: "O Great Rain-God, you have saved our lives. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: "O people, do not speak thus. I am here to extinguish the fire of the three poisons within all beings. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having comforted the inhabitants of the city, taught them the Dharma. Having taught them the Dharma, he established them in the realization of the emptiness of all phenomena. This is the fifth instance of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s power of skillful means. ||| [60,vi] ||| Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the lower regions, beheld a great ocean that was turbulent and dangerous. Seeing it, he manifested himself as a great ship and crossed over it. When the merchants and sailors saw the great ship, they were filled with joy and said: "O Great Ship, you have carried us across the sea of birth and death. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: "O people, do not speak thus. I am here to carry all beings across the ocean of saṃsāra to the shore of nirvāṇa. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having comforted the merchants and sailors, taught them the Dharma. Having taught them the Dharma, he established them in the attainment of the wisdom of omniscience. This is the sixth instance of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s power of skillful means. ||| [60,vii] ||| Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the intermediate regions, beheld a starving tigress who was on the verge of devouring her own cubs. Seeing her, he manifested himself as a deer and offered his body to her. When the tigress saw the deer, she was filled with hunger and devoured it. When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara saw that the tigress had eaten the deer, he restored his original form and stood before her. Seeing the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the tigress was filled with awe and said: "O Great Being, you have saved the lives of my cubs. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: "O mother, do not speak thus. I am here to save all beings from the hunger of craving. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having comforted the tigress, taught her the Dharma. Having taught her the Dharma, he established her in the state of non-harming toward all living beings. This is the seventh instance of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s power of skillful means. ||| [60,viii] ||| Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the realm of the asuras, beheld a great battle between the asuras and the gods. Seeing it, he manifested himself as a peacock and entered the midst of the battle. When the asuras saw the peacock, they were terrified and retreated. When the gods saw the peacock, they were filled with joy and said: "O Great Peacock, you have protected us

Now, it is indeed perceived that "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) refers to an object that is to be accomplished (*kārya*). Yet, that [object] does not exist as something yet-to-be (*bhaviṣyan*), because there is no means of knowledge (*māna*) for it and because it cannot be determined with certainty. Precisely because it is something to be accomplished, it does not persist into other times. Nor is it non-existent, because it is perceived. This has already been answered: if [the object] possesses its own nature (*sātmakatva*), there is no real distinction of time; if [the distinction] is from the perspective of cognition (*pramiti*), then there is no distinction in the object itself—thus, [the object] is devoid of intrinsic reality (*nairātmya*). How, then, is there perception? For this very reason, the learned hold that verbal cognition is merely a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*) or mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is based upon intuition. Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when supported by intuition, constitute the constituent elements of worldly activity.
Furthermore—
Thus, there is this doubt regarding the meaning of the Veda:
that the mandate (niyoga) is not something to be performed, and the activity of one who is mandated is not bound solely by the mandate.

Indeed, that which is neither past, nor present, nor future—that is, whose single certainty is not determined—is the object of doubtful cognition (*āśaṅkā-jñāna*). For example, when rain has not yet fallen and has not yet begun, its single certainty remains undetermined because it enters the path of perception through the power of seeing the rising of exceedingly dark and dense clouds, despite the observation of deviation [from the expected outcome]. Alas, the meaning of the Veda has been brought to this very state by those possessed of wisdom through their excessive exegesis.

Furthermore, the object (*kārya*) is not the mandate (*niyoga*). And the object is what is to be known through the Veda, because other word-meanings are subordinate to it. It is that very object which must be expressed in order to establish its independence—since it is not within the scope of other means of knowledge—with respect to the distinction of time. [Objection: But surely the cognition of "being an object" (*kāryyatva*) is precisely the mandate itself; for people designate it thus: "The teacher's mandate is to be performed," or "The king's command is to be executed. [Reply: This is not so, because it would follow that the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is the enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*). For the agent of a mandate is the enjoiner. Moreover, from where does the mandate derive the status of being an object to be performed in the case of a sacrifice? For this [mandate] is not enjoined upon that [sacrifice].

[62,i] That [action] must be performed as its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and there is no dependence on anything else therein, unlike the case of the object. However, the phrase "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) would then mean "one should cause [another] to sacrifice" (*yājayet*). And thus, one who desires heaven would have fulfilled the purpose of the scripture merely by enjoining another; in this way, your honor has most effectively accomplished what was intended! Furthermore, if the object to be performed were the *niyoga* (the mandate), then heaven and the sacrifice would be mutually unrelated, because they would not be connected to that [mandate].

[63,i] Because of the restriction, as in the case of the red cow and the one-year-old heifer, which are connected by a single injunction. True; there is no injunction for sacrifice for one who desires something else, and the injunction for one who desires heaven does not apply elsewhere than to the sacrifice. However, the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is untenable.

Now, it may be argued that an injunction (*niyoga*) is not capable of making known what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) unless it effects a relationship between the object and the person enjoined, for it lacks the necessary form. Indeed, the very nature of an injunction is that "it enjoins someone to something," such that "this must be done by this person. Furthermore, a relationship is not possible without a relation of primary and subordinate status; thus, since heaven is not for the sake of another, the sacrifice must be for its sake, because when something is connected with what is desired, it is understood to be in service to that end. Granted that the injunction effects the connection between the person enjoined and the object, how does it bring about the connection between the object and the qualifiers of the person enjoined?

If it is argued that this is due to a specific relationship, then the same would apply to livelihood and so forth as well. What follows from this? Does the occasion (nimitta) possess the status of a subordinate factor (aṅgatva) or the status of a primary factor (prādhānya)? If it were a subordinate factor, there would be the consequence of its extension (atideśa) by analogy.

If primacy were granted [to the qualification], there would be no distinction between the entitlements for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites; since both would be directed toward the task to be accomplished (*kārya*), the occasional rite would not be restricted to the performance itself. Consequently, in both cases, there would be either the inclusion of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) or their exclusion. Furthermore, once its purpose is fulfilled by providing the specific person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the life-span (*jīvana*) and so forth could no longer be connected to the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of the injunction. The relationship of cause (*nimitta*) and effect (*naimittika*) would then be merely implied. And if that were the case, one might as well argue that even in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), the same would apply because the person is entitled [by virtue of being alive]. But this will not be so, because the qualification is precisely of that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), owing to its being something desired (*kāmya*). Even so, there is no proof for a connection with the subject matter; for it is possible for something else to be the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) while still serving as a qualification, and because we observe that it is merely a desire (*icchā*) that is seen. [Objection: The understanding of the entitlement of one who desires belongs properly to the means to that desire, and not otherwise; for if it were otherwise, the act would be performed by someone other than the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). [Response: An act performed by one who desires would indeed be performed by the person to be enjoined.

Desire, however, is not the cause of activity; rather, it is the cause of entitlement (*adhikāra*). And activity is held to be caused by entitlement, not caused by the fruit, because prior to the entitlement, that [fruit] is unknown.

[66,i] But surely, it is those possessed of desire who have the qualification (*adhikāra*). And since desire does not exist in the absence of a means, it cannot be that the qualification has no cause; nor can it have any cause other than desire. It has desire as its cause, because one is qualified only when that desire exists.

Now, for one who is enjoined toward what is not a means, the desire for the fruit is not the cause [of the injunction]. For it is the desire for the goal (the end) that is the cause of the injunction regarding the means. In that case, the injunction occurs once the relationship between the means and the goal is already established; it is not from the injunction that their establishment arises. [Objection: That relationship is understood precisely because of the injunction. [Reply: No, because it would involve dependence on something else. To explain: if the meaning of the word is an injunction directed toward a specific person, how can that [relationship] be known from the injunction? Or, if the injunction is caused by a specific fruit, then since that [fruit] does not exist prior to the establishment of that relationship, the word would have to express it as depending on a previously established state of affairs; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence of the word’s dependence on another means of knowledge (pramāṇāntara).
Furthermore,
if the goal itself were the cause for entitlement, there would be no entitlement in cases such as "as long as one lives" (jīvanādi).

Furthermore, this [position] is untenable because there is no word expressing the cause for the cognition of the occasioning condition (*nimitta*). Rather, when that [condition] exists, it is called an "occasioning condition" by implication (*arthāt*) because it qualifies the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) within the mandate (*niyoga*). If terms such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) were intended solely to express the occasioning condition, they would not then be intended to express the person to be enjoined. In that case, since no qualification (*adhikāra*) would be perceived, there would be no performance of the rite. If, on the other hand, the qualification is established by implication, then the rejection of the position that [the term] qualifies the agent (*kartṛ*) is superfluous.

[68, ii] For just as the qualification (*adhikāra*) is understood through desire with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which serves as the means (*upāya*), so too agency (*kartṛtva*) is not a non-means through desire; and for whom there is a means to the desired object, for him this is the action (*karman*). Thus, by implication, the establishment of qualification follows from the injunction that restricts the agent. Just as in the case of an injunction of qualification, the restriction of the agent is established. Furthermore, in a sentence connected with a desired end, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is with the desired object, not with the mandate (*niyoga*); for if it were connected with both objects, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). [69, i]

Now, it may be objected that an injunction (*niyoga*) does not sublate the application (*viniyoga*), because there is no contradiction between them; for the cognition of those [factors] occurs precisely according to their application. In that case, the word-meanings, mutually connected, become the objects of the injunction. And this connection cannot exist without a relationship of subordinate and principal. Since [heaven] is desired, heaven is the principal and the ritual action is subordinate. Thus, a person desiring heaven is enjoined with respect to the ritual action as a subordinate element; therefore, the primacy of the injunction is not lost, and the connection between the ritual action and its fruit is established.

Furthermore, the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) does not spontaneously engage in the pursuit of desire, because even one who desires [the object] does not act when the means are lacking. Nor can there be knowledge of the means and the end prior to the injunction; for it is not accepted that the connection between heaven and sacrifice is based on a specific application (*viniyoga*). That [connection] belongs to the third [chapter], whereas this [injunction] belongs to the section on the mandate (*naiyogikī*). Moreover, the claim that the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is the object of the mandate would be directly contradicted. Furthermore, there would be a lack of qualification (*niradhikāratā*), because the object of the action is the cause of qualification; otherwise, one would fail to postulate such a qualification in cases like the Viśvajit sacrifice. There is a contradiction between being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and being defined by its nature [as an end], due to the distinction between what is already established and what is not. Additionally, since the agent's status arises through the connection [to the action] prior to the mandate, there would be no status as one to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*) before that mandate. Finally, there would be the undesirable consequence of the action being mandatory regardless of desire, because desire would not be the governing factor; even if it were the governing factor, the mere wish would itself have to be performed as a necessity. Therefore, the connection with the mandate occurs only between two things that are mutually unrelated [prior to it]. If they were so connected, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Even the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) has been refuted on the grounds of their connection to a single mandate.

[71,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as real. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha as real. He does not perceive the Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata as real. Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real.”

But surely, it is understood from the *niyoga* (injunction) that "this is beneficial to this [agent]"; how then could it be the *karman* (the object/task) of that [injunction]? What kind of benefit could it provide other than being something desired (*kāmya*)? If there were some other benefit, the word "seeker" (*arthin*) would be meaningless. If, then, the meaning of the *niyoga* is simply the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, what follows from this? Its status as an *upadeśaka* (an original, prescriptive teaching) would be lost; furthermore, because it would merely be a restatement of an existing fact, it would be dependent on something else. Therefore, the meaning of the *niyoga* is "this must be done by him," because the cognition of performance arises [from it] and because it is non-deviant [in its application]. This is not the case for the *adhikāra* (qualification) based on an occasion (*naimittika*) or a prohibition (*niṣedha*), since they do not rely on a [direct] benefit. Nor is the *niyoga* restricted to an action solely for the sake of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). For this very reason, it is absent in worldly cases such as requests (*adhyeṣaṇā*). But surely, heaven (*svarga*) is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Let it be so that it is connected to the *niyoga*; however, the *niyoga* itself does not establish the connection with the sacrifice. Rather, it is expressed thus: "such a person is enjoined. It is just like the statement: "He whose house fire burns... But surely, if the *bhāvārtha* (the meaning of the verbal root) is the means to achieve the desired end, then the accomplishment of the fruit would follow from the *niyoga*? It would be so if the *bhāvārtha* were of such a nature; but it is not, as has been stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka*.

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as 'a dharma'? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even a minute dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as 'a dharma. Therefore, Blessed One, the Tathāgata speaks of 'the dharma of the dharma,' 'the reality-limit of the dharma,' and 'the nature of the dharma. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the dharma-eye? Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. The Tathāgata possesses the dharma-eye. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye? Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? The Tathāgata possesses the eye of the knowledge of the aspects of all modes of the Buddhas of the present. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? The Tathāgata possesses the eye of the knowledge of the aspects of all modes of the Buddhas of the ten directions. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the eye of the knowledge of the aspects of all modes of the Buddhas of the three times? Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. Does the Tathāgata possess the eye of the knowledge of the aspects of all modes of the Buddhas of the three times and the ten directions, including those who have attained parinirvāṇa, and does he know them? Furthermore, there would be the consequence of [an independent] result even for a causal rite (*naimittika*). How, in this view, there is no connection between action and its fruit has been explained in the *Bhāvanāviveka*. Therefore, because there is no relation between heaven and sacrifice, there is no knowledge of a means to achieve a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). And it is those who are discerning who desire to know the means to achieve a human goal. Moreover, since the meaning of words is understood from common worldly usage, the injunction (*niyoga*) is not primary; for there is no injunction once that [result] is established. Nor does the cognizer apprehend it [the injunction], because even when the object is established, there is no performance [of the act]. For in the command "Bring the cow," what is intended by the speaker is not the establishment of the injunction itself, but rather the establishment of the object.

[74,i] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by his great compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from their suffering. Thereupon, the Bhagavān addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “If there be any sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall single-mindedly keep it in mind, then I declare that such persons will be delivered from all calamities. If they should fall into a great fire, by virtue of keeping the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind, that fire shall not be able to burn them. If they should fall into a great torrent of water, by virtue of keeping the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind, they shall not drown, but shall quickly reach the shore of safety. If there be many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of robbers who intend to plunder and harm a certain person, and if that person should single-mindedly call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s spiritual protection, the bandits shall not be able to harm them. Thus spoke the Bhagavān. Having spoken thus, the World-Honored One further addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, if there be any sons or daughters of good family who wish to worship and make offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata, they should fashion images of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, whether made of precious gems, or of gold, silver, bronze, iron, clay, lacquer, or wood; or they may paint them on walls or cloth, using various colors. Whether they be made of precious substances or painted, they should be fashioned with a body like that of a youth, adorned with a jeweled crown, holding a lotus flower in the hand, and standing upright. If one fashions such an image and makes offerings to it, one shall obtain immeasurable merit. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassionate power and can deliver sentient beings from immeasurable sufferings. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Bhagavān: “Bhagavān, what is the reason for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara being called ‘Avalokiteśvara’? The Bhagavān replied to the Venerable Ānanda: “If there be any sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall single-mindedly keep it in mind, then I declare that such persons will be delivered from all calamities. Therefore, Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is called ‘Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there be any sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall single-mindedly keep it in mind, then I declare that such persons will be delivered from all calamities. For this reason, Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is called ‘Avalokiteśvara. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Bhagavān: “Bhagavān, how should one practice the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s samādhi? The Bhagavān replied to the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, if there be any sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s samādhi, they should first purify their minds, dwell in a quiet place, and contemplate the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s form. They should visualize him as having a body like a youth, adorned with a jeweled crown, holding a lotus flower, and standing upright. Having visualized this form, they should recite the mantra: ‘Namaḥ sarva-jñāya, tadyathā, gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. If they recite this mantra eight hundred times, they shall immediately see the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara before them, and their hearts shall be filled with joy. If they wish to hear the Dharma, they shall hear the Dharma; if they wish to see the Buddhas, they shall see the Buddhas; if they wish to be born in the Pure Land, they shall be born in the Pure Land. For this reason, Ānanda, you should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is indeed a great compassionate benefactor to all sentient beings. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, were filled with joy and practiced accordingly. Thus ends the chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the seventy-fourth.

The function of words in the world is one thing, and in the Veda it is another. For in the world, the syntactical connection (*samanvaya*) of words is intent upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), whereas in the Veda it is intent upon an injunction (*niyoga*). This is like a boil upon a tumor. If, indeed, the capacity of words is understood from worldly usage to be intent upon the speaker’s intention, then they cannot be intent upon anything else; for the capacity of words has no other source of authority than this. If it is argued that there is no speaker (in the case of the Veda), then it follows that this very syntactical connection intent upon the speaker’s intention would itself lead to the inference of such a speaker, and thus the Veda would be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). Alternatively, there would be no comprehension [of meaning], or if comprehension does occur, it would not be caused by the words themselves, but would be either conventional (*sāmayikī*) or produced by inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭajā*). Therefore, your esteemed self’s delusion—that the injunction (*niyoga*) is the "thing to be done" (*kārya*)—is born solely from figurative usage. Moreover, in the world, an injunction alone is not the cause of activity, since everyone does not act merely because of an injunction. Activity occurs only when there is an injunction from one who is to be obeyed (*anuvidheya*). And the cause of obedience is the attainment of what is beneficial or the avoidance of what is harmful, which is established by other means of knowledge. Furthermore, there is no one to issue the injunction even in the Veda; how much less, then, can there be one to be obeyed? If it is argued that the Word itself is the one to be obeyed, let it be the issuer of the injunction, but it cannot be the one to be obeyed, for there is no reason for it. There is no proof that one must obey the word regarding the attainment or avoidance of benefit and harm. If you say it is the injunction (*niyoga*), no; for that is the object of knowledge (*prameya*). If you say it is the *knowledge* of the injunction, no; for that has the injunction as its object, and the injunction is distinct from those two (the word and its cognition). Nor can it be implied by the sense of the matter, because we see injunctions issued by untrustworthy persons, such as: "This path is safe; may you go by this very way. In the world, an injunction is grounded in the connection of word-meanings (*padārthānvaya*), and since that is the domain of other means of knowledge, worldly activity depends upon them and is caused by them. But in the Veda, it is said to be grounded in the injunction alone; therefore, it requires nothing else. This has already been answered. Moreover, an injunction alone is not the cause of activity. If so, then the knowledge of the injunction is false. But that is not tenable, due to the absence of two causes [for falsity]. We do not deny the existence of the injunction, which would make it false. Even while it exists, a person acts in the world simply by the command of anyone at all. It is not that there is no injunction there. It was stated that if the injunction were not intent upon that [benefit/harm], then its purport (*tātparya*) would lack authority. If it is argued that activity arises from the understanding of "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*), and that one who is enjoined understands, "This is my duty," then consider one who, though understanding, does not perform the task: he is not restrained by punishments, just as one who does not act despite knowing the attainment or avoidance of benefit and harm. This view fails to examine the true nature of the injunction. To explain: an injunction is merely an impulsion (*pravartanā*), and since that is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) etc., the verbal cognition is "I am impelled here. The understanding of "what is to be done," however, arises from the fact that the issuer of the injunction is one to be obeyed; for when there is an injunction from one to be obeyed, one determines, "This is my duty. In other cases, there is only the cognition of the impulsion. And it has been said: "The injunction has 'what is to be done' as its object, but the injunction does not state that 'what is to be done' is its own nature. If you say that the understanding of "what is to be done" arises precisely because the injunction has that as its object, that is not a verbal [cognition], since the word expresses only the injunction. Nor is it a result of the sense (*ārtha*), because it is absent in all injunctions. Therefore, the elders do not favor this view, as it is attractive only when not scrutinized. Let it be, then, that there is an issuer of the injunction for living beings—one who has directly perceived the means to the welfare taught in the scriptures, who desires our well-being, and who is omniscient.
No; because that [valid cognition] is untenable and due to ignorance. For it is thus:
since there is no effect in the absence of a cause, when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exist, there is no valid cognition (*pramā*).
The external objects of the eye and so forth, as previously described, are the dependent nature (paratantra); the mind is likewise external.

[81,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling is empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling; perception is empty of the intrinsic nature of perception; formations are empty of the intrinsic nature of formations; consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness. Subhūti, because they are empty of intrinsic nature, these five aggregates are called ‘empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye; the ear is empty of the intrinsic nature of the ear; the nose is empty of the intrinsic nature of the nose; the tongue is empty of the intrinsic nature of the tongue; the body is empty of the intrinsic nature of the body; the mind is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind. Subhūti, because they are empty of intrinsic nature, these six internal bases are called ‘empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, forms are empty of the intrinsic nature of forms; sounds are empty of the intrinsic nature of sounds; odors are empty of the intrinsic nature of odors; tastes are empty of the intrinsic nature of tastes; tangibles are empty of the intrinsic nature of tangibles; mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of mental phenomena. Subhūti, because they are empty of intrinsic nature, these six external bases are called ‘empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, eye-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness; ear-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of ear-consciousness; nose-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of nose-consciousness; tongue-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of tongue-consciousness; body-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of body-consciousness; mind-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of mind-consciousness. Subhūti, because they are empty of intrinsic nature, these six consciousnesses are called ‘empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of contact; feeling is empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling; craving is empty of the intrinsic nature of craving; grasping is empty of the intrinsic nature of grasping; becoming is empty of the intrinsic nature of becoming; birth is empty of the intrinsic nature of birth; old age and death are empty of the intrinsic nature of old age and death. Subhūti, because they are empty of intrinsic nature, these twelve links of dependent origination are called ‘empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of giving is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving; the perfection of morality is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of morality; the perfection of patience is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience; the perfection of vigor is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of vigor; the perfection of meditation is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of meditation; the perfection of wisdom is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, because they are empty of intrinsic nature, these six perfections are called ‘empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, the emptiness of the internal is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the internal; the emptiness of the external is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the external; the emptiness of the internal and external is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the internal and external; the emptiness of emptiness is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of emptiness; the great emptiness is empty of the intrinsic nature of the great emptiness; the emptiness of ultimate reality is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of ultimate reality; the emptiness of conditioned phenomena is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of conditioned phenomena; the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena; the absolute emptiness is empty of the intrinsic nature of the absolute emptiness; Although the cessation of one's own perception does not necessarily entail the non-existence of things that are remote, the cessation of all perceptions is unproven (*asiddha*). Furthermore, for one who is not omniscient, the non-existence of an object cannot be established merely by the cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the absence of the pervader (*avyāpaka*) does not invariably entail the absence of the pervaded (*avyāpya*). This lack of pervasion is due to the fact that [perception] is not the cause [of existence], and because there is no necessary concomitance (*tanmātrānubandha*) between them; otherwise, it would follow that everyone is omniscient, as there would be no distinction [between individuals]. Moreover, although speech and other such signs do not preclude [the existence of objects] because they are not contradictory to it, we nevertheless infer the absence of the consciousness of all objects—which is the effect of those [signs]—on the grounds that the means of valid cognition are untenable. For we perceive the cessation of the effect through the cessation of its cause. Specifically, perception arising from the eyes and other senses does not apply to all objects, because their range of objects is restricted. Indeed, only certain present and connected things are their objects, not all things.

[82,i] Furthermore, although a restriction by way of form (*rūpa*) is difficult to establish because of the perception of manifold objects of cognition, there is no restriction of connection by way of place (*deśa*), because there is a discernment of objects located in various places and possessing various dimensions due to distinctions such as intensity and dullness. Nor is there a restriction by way of dimension (*parimāṇa*). However, restriction by way of time (*kāla*) is now examined: for if [the sense organ] functions by reaching [the object], there is no reaching of that which is not present; and even if it functions without reaching [the object], it nonetheless depends upon the causal capacity of the object.

Because that which has not yet arisen and that which has already ceased are inexpressible and lack causal capacity at the time of the arising of cognition. Thus, even in the case of superior capacities, the eyes and other sense organs would perceive their own objects only as exceeding them in terms of location, magnitude, or number, but never an object that is not their domain, one that has not yet arisen, or one that has already passed away. This is stated because perception is the apprehension of what is presently existing. For instance, in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) involving the cognition of color and so forth, that cognition is dependent upon the eyes and other senses; it is restricted precisely by their restriction. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-existence of the blind and the deaf. Mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) also has internal objects such as pleasure and the like for its domain, because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects. It has been stated that if it were independent, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and others. [Objection: If the non-existence of the blind and others does not follow because of the dependence on the auxiliary condition of the immediately preceding cognition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) from which that [mental perception] arises, then in every respect, dependence is not removed, since it still depends on that [preceding cognition]. [Reply: Because it has that as its object. Otherwise, even if it were assisted by something produced by another sense organ, the same undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the blind and others would persist. Furthermore, the immediately preceding cognition does not have an object of the same class (*jāti*), because there is no transition between different classes. Indeed, this is not a property of cognition, because there is a transition between different classes; nor is it a property of perception, because it depends on forms and so forth that have not been conceptualized (*avitarkita*); nor is it a property of mental perception, because it is not observed in the case of pleasure and the like. Moreover, let there be dependence due to the restriction of the object, or let it be due to the dependence on a specific auxiliary condition, for such dependence is seen in the case of memory. Furthermore, if [the mental perception] were to grasp a similar form within the range of a single sense organ, there would be the undesirable consequence of grasping another form simultaneously. If it were to depend on an intermediate class, there would be the fallacy of it belonging to a different continuum (*saṃtāna*), because there is no difference in class between what occurs in that continuum and what does not. Therefore, by one who asserts that the immediately preceding cognition belongs to a single continuum-moment, it is effectively said that it must grasp the object of the eye and other senses. This is because, while there is the appearance of a distinction between moments, there is no appearance of identity, and thus momentariness is rejected.

[99,i] The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, the person who is like a white lotus flower, and the person who is like a fragrant lotus flower. What, monks, is the person who is like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a low family—whether a family of outcastes, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or waste-removers—and is poor, destitute, and lacking in livelihood; he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored, with a dark complexion, afflicted by many illnesses, and weak in strength. Yet, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, he dwells detached from sensual pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, having attained the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of detachment, and filled with joy and bliss. He dwells having attained the second dhyāna, which is free from thought and examination, inwardly serene, mentally unified, and devoid of thought and examination, born of concentration, and filled with joy and bliss. He dwells having attained the third dhyāna, which is free from joy, equanimous, mindful, and clearly conscious, experiencing bliss with the body, which the Noble Ones describe as ‘dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss. He dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. This, monks, is called the person who is like a lotus flower. Why is that? Because, monks, although this person is born into a low family, poor, destitute, and lacking in livelihood; although he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored, with a dark complexion, afflicted by many illnesses, and weak in strength; yet, through the attainment of these four dhyānas, he becomes one who is highly esteemed, honored, and revered by the world of gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and by the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, gods and humans. Just as a lotus flower, though born in the mud and water, rises above the water and stands unsullied by the water, so too, monks, this person is called a ‘lotus-like person’ because, although born into a low family and possessing those aforementioned qualities, through the attainment of these four dhyānas, he becomes one who is highly esteemed, honored, and revered by the world of gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and by the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, gods and humans. This, monks, is called the person who is like a lotus flower. And what, monks, is the person who is like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a high family—whether a family of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, or householders—and is wealthy, affluent, and possessing abundant wealth and grain; he is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, with a fair complexion, free from many illnesses, and strong in strength. Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, he dwells detached from sensual pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, having attained the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of detachment, and filled with joy and bliss. He dwells having attained the second dhyāna, which is free from thought and examination, inwardly serene, mentally unified, and devoid of thought and examination, born of concentration, and filled with joy and bliss. He dwells having attained the third dhyāna, which is free from joy, equanimous, mindful, and clearly conscious, experiencing bliss with the body, which the Noble Ones describe as ‘dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss. He dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. This, monks, is called the person who is like a blue lotus flower. Why is that? Because, monks, this person is born into a high family, wealthy, affluent, and possessing abundant wealth and grain; he is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, with a fair complexion, free from many illnesses, and strong in strength. Through the attainment of these four dhyānas, he becomes one who is highly esteemed, honored, and revered by the world of gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and by the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, gods and humans. Just as a blue lotus flower, though born in the water, remains on the surface and is not sullied by the water, so too, monks, this person is called a ‘blue-lotus-like person’ because, although born into a high family and possessing those aforementioned qualities, through the attainment of these four dhyānas, he becomes one who is highly esteemed, honored, and revered by the world of gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and by the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, gods and humans. This, monks, is called the person who is like a blue lotus flower. And what, monks, is the person who is like a white lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a high family—whether a family of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, or householders—and is wealthy, affluent, and possessing abundant wealth and grain; he is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, with a fair complexion, free from many illnesses, and strong in strength. Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, he dwells detached from sensual pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, having attained the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of detachment, and filled with joy and bliss. He dwells having attained the second dhyāna, which is free from thought and examination, inwardly serene, mentally unified, and devoid of thought and examination, born of concentration, and filled with joy and bliss. He dwells having attained the third dhyāna, which is free from joy, equanimous, mindful, and clearly conscious, experiencing bliss with the body, which the Noble Ones describe as ‘dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss. He dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. Furthermore, he attains the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñānadarśana). This, monks, is called the person who is like a white lotus flower. Why is that? Because, monks, this person is born into a high family, wealthy, affluent, and possessing abundant wealth and grain; he is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, with a fair complexion, free from many illnesses, and strong in strength. Through the attainment of these four dhyānas and the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the outflows, he becomes one who is highly esteemed, honored, and revered by the world of gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and by the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, gods and humans. Just as a white lotus flower, though born in the water, rises above the water and stands unsullied by the water, so too, monks, this person is called a ‘white-lotus-like person’ because, although born into a high family and possessing those aforementioned qualities, through the attainment of these four dhyānas and the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the outflows, he becomes one who is highly esteemed, honored, and revered by the world of gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and by the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, gods and humans.
