Moreover, since there is no perception of color and so forth when there is a defect in the mind (*manas*) or an absence of the eyes and other senses, it is determined that [the object] is perceivable by both. But how could there be perception by the mind alone? If it is argued that this is because [the object] is perceived in the second moment, we say no; for in that case, there is no reason for the capacity of the eyes and other senses to have failed, and because we observe a continuous stream of cognitions regarding that [object]. As for memory, its dependence [on prior perception] is indeed established; and in inference and the like, dependence is evident because cognition occurs even in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth. Thus, the mind never functions independently and directly with respect to an external [object]. Therefore, only an internal object is the direct domain, and only therein would the mind experience excellence through its direct operation, not in what is not its domain.

Even the consciousness consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-vijñāna*) has as its objects that which was previously heard or inferred; since cultivation cannot occur spontaneously, it is dependent upon scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*). Because it conforms to the truth-value or falsity of the prior cognition, and because it is thus dependent, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

[108,i] But surely there is no restriction upon the eyes and other sense-faculties even with respect to time, since there is the perception of silver and such things that are not present. For that is not a perception of mother-of-pearl and the like; for it is impossible for a cognition having one form to have something else as its object, as that would lead to a lack of reliability.
[109,i] And in a dream, the mind has attained independence; yet dream-cognition is not memory, because it does not possess the nature of that [memory]. This is not sound. For instance:
The expectation of an external object is futile, as the manifestation of another form is equal [to that of an object];
for even the vivid memory of a person's present existence in a dream is indeed [a cognition of] something non-existent.

[109,ii] First of all, the eye and other sense organs manifest only a present object, such as a fragment of mother-of-pearl, because they depend upon it; otherwise, their proximity would be fruitless, since the cognition of silver would occur even in the absence of that object. <ed_110> If the appearance of silverness does not have the mother-of-pearl as its object, then the manifestation of the present likewise cannot have something non-present as its domain.

The fact that [an object] appears as such due to a defect applies equally to the other case as well. Furthermore, the appearance of what is not present occurs when something is present, whereas the appearance of what is present does not occur when something is absent; this is because the proximity of an object must be fruitful. Moreover, the negation "this is not silver" is logically possible only when there has been a prior apprehension of silver. In the case of a person with ophthalmia (*taimirika*) seeing a mass of hair in fragments of light, the deviation from reality is not dependent on an external object. In dreams as well, is it the memory that appears as present, or is it the independence of the mind? It is more reasonable that it is the memory appearing as present. This is because one clearly remembers—without omission or addition—the experience of the immediately preceding day, perceiving it as if it were present due to the influence of a defect. However, the independence of the mind is not observed [in ordinary experience]. Nor does a defect produce an excess of capacity, since a defect is a cause for the removal of capacity. If a dream-vision is true because it apprehends a present object in that way, then that is unobserved. If it is argued that it is observed because one sees a correspondence with the objects described upon waking, we say no; for there is no necessary correspondence with the description. Any correspondence with the description is merely accidental (*kākatālīya*). But how can the perception of a future event as if it were present be true? Let it not be true; nevertheless, the independence of the mind exists. That too is simply the recollection of a twofold experienced object. Otherwise, one would have to postulate an unobserved capacity for the mind. If it were a specific merit (*dharma*), it would result in the perception of things exactly as they are; for its effect would require the postulation of an unobserved capacity. If dream-cognition is not memory, then it is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) either, because there is no external object to be grasped in that way. If that is so, the mind is not independent regarding external objects, since in a dream that [external object] is not being grasped. Or, if it is grasped, it is the grasping of what was previously experienced, for that is how it is seen. One should not postulate an excess of unobserved capacity due to a defect; thus, in both ways, the mind is not independent regarding the external world. By this, the vision of hair and so forth by one with ophthalmia is also refuted.
In the world, intuition arising from fallacious signs and the like is non-conclusive;
it occurs when cognition is entirely complete, and never when it is deficient.

[119, ii] Furthermore, it is said that when one has the intuition, "My brother will come tomorrow," the mind is seen to be independent of external objects because it lacks dependence on sense-organs, signs, and so forth. Moreover, whether it be the claim that "everything is everything," or that existent and non-existent categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so on, or primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the self (*puruṣa*), the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and so forth—regardless of their distinctions—are objects of the mind by virtue of worldly authority; thus, even in its independence, the mind's omniscience regarding external things is established. To this, it is replied:

To begin with, supramundane *pratibhāna* (intuition) is a subject of dispute. Mundane *pratibhāna*, however, has as its object the pleasant and the unpleasant, and generally arises from the appearance of signs such as the clarity or agitation of the heart that occur simultaneously; for this very reason, it is designated as *pratibhāna* itself and not as "certainty" (*niścaya*), because it is essentially non-definitive. Yet, because it touches upon both alternatives and is [in that regard] equal, it is not of the nature of doubt (*saṃśaya*). It is simply *pratibhā*. It is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its result is non-certainty and because its certainty depends on another means of knowledge. Likewise, because it depends on the class of signs (*liṅga*) and so forth, there is dependence (*pāratantrya*) even in that case. Otherwise, if the mind were independent of those and could establish external objects by its own power alone, then for everyone, everything would always be present to everyone. Furthermore, if the mind—due to a particular unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*)—were to operate toward an external object without depending on the senses or signs, there would be the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the eyes and other organs are useless. Moreover, since all cognitions would be established from that very same particular unseen force, the [external] instruments would also be useless. Since the agent, the self, who is himself without instruments, achieves the act of determination solely through a particular unseen force, the unseen force alone would accomplish the purpose. Indeed, even an unseen force does not accomplish an object without a means, given the necessity of initiating the body and so forth. Therefore, the operation of the mind is not inherently independent of the senses, signs, and so forth. For this very reason, mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) regarding all objects does not arise from merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), because the establishment of that perception requires the means of sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*). This is because we do not admit "conjunction with what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*). Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of perceiving objects obstructed by walls and the like, and there would be the consequence of inference being nothing but perception. Furthermore, such perception would be impossible in the case of things unborn or already passed away. For this very reason, there is no contact between the sense organ and the object when both are established [as existing]; for past and future things do not exist even then, which would lead to the consequence of perceiving obstructed objects, and there would be the consequence of inference and so forth being perception. Also, the mention of "contact" (*sannikarṣa*) in the definition would be redundant. Now, one might argue: "Since past and future things are known as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of space and so forth, and since cognition has as its objective support (*ālambana*) specific spaces etc., contact between the eye or the mind and those [spaces] is possible. And since they exist and are present, the status of cognition of things unborn or passed away as being produced by contact between sense organ and object remains unimpeded. And since the definitions of inference and so forth are absent, 'cognition produced by contact between sense organ and object' does not apply to inference and the rest. If, first, "any object whatsoever" is meant, then memory (*smṛti*) would have the consequence of being perception. If, on the other hand, "the object of knowledge" (*prameya*) is meant, let the cognition of space and so forth be perception, because of contact with that much; but the cognition of the qualifier is not. If it is argued that "since qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is perception, by implication the qualifier is also perception," [we reply: no, because there is no contact with that [qualifier]. For if the qualifier is absent, the qualified thing does not exist, even if it is present; otherwise, everything would be so. How then is Devadatta’s son, Yajñadatta, called such when his mother has passed away? What is the point here? It is not that he enters into linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) as being qualified by her at that time. If, then, a non-present thing is not a factor in linguistic usage, then Devadatta too would not be a factor in linguistic usage as a qualifier. If linguistic usage occurs by means of a former qualifier, then the same applies to the qualified state; it is not barred by a staff [if the staff is gone]. Such a qualifier is not a "mere indicator" (*upalakṣaṇa*), because it is distinct in form and not present. The difference between these two is indeed caused by presence and absence. Therefore, a qualified thing is not present when its qualifier is absent. If the qualifier is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and the genus (*jāti*) and so forth are also objects of knowledge, then perception would result even without contact with an object; but it is not so, because the definition lacks that [contact], since the sense organ depends on an object.

[124,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that would constitute a bodhisattva. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor forms, nor eye-consciousness; nor the ear, nor sounds, nor ear-consciousness; nor the nose, nor odors, nor nose-consciousness; nor the tongue, nor tastes, nor tongue-consciousness; nor the body, nor tangibles, nor body-consciousness; nor the mind, nor mental phenomena, nor mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the aggregate of form, nor the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness. He does not perceive the sense-field of the eye, nor the sense-fields of forms, eye-consciousness, or contact; nor the sense-fields of the ear, sounds, ear-consciousness, or contact; nor the sense-fields of the nose, odors, nose-consciousness, or contact; nor the sense-fields of the tongue, tastes, tongue-consciousness, or contact; nor the sense-fields of the body, tangibles, body-consciousness, or contact; nor the sense-fields of the mind, mental phenomena, mind-consciousness, or contact. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm. He does not perceive the conditioned, nor the unconditioned. He does not perceive the past, nor the future, nor the present. He does not perceive the stream-enterer, nor the fruit of stream-entry; nor the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; nor the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; nor the arhat, nor the fruit of arhatship; nor the pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the perfection of giving, nor the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, nor the emptiness of the external, nor the emptiness of the internal and external; nor the emptiness of emptiness, nor the great emptiness, nor the emptiness of the ultimate; nor the emptiness of the conditioned, nor the emptiness of the unconditioned, nor the emptiness of the limitless; nor the emptiness of dispersion, nor the emptiness of nature, nor the emptiness of all dharmas; nor the emptiness of own-marks, nor the emptiness of non-existence, nor the emptiness of existence; nor the emptiness of non-attainment, nor the emptiness of essential nature, nor the emptiness of the essential nature of non-essential nature. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor the four grounds of self-confidence, nor the four analytical knowledges, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He does not perceive the path of the śrāvaka, nor the path of the pratyekabuddha, nor the path of the bodhisattva. He does not perceive omniscience, nor the knowledge of the paths, nor the knowledge of all aspects. He does not perceive the level of a śrāvaka, nor the level of a pratyekabuddha, nor the level of a bodhisattva, nor the level of a Tathāgata. He does not perceive the stage of dry wisdom, nor the stage of the heat of wisdom, nor the stage of the summit of wisdom, nor the stage of patient acceptance, nor the stage of the worldly supreme dharmas, nor the stage of the dharmas of penetration, nor the stage of the dharmas of the path of seeing, nor the stage of the dharmas of the path of cultivation, nor the stage of the dharmas of the path of no-more-learning. He does not perceive the stage of a stream-enterer, nor the stage of a once-returner, nor the stage of a non-returner, nor the stage of an arhat, nor the stage of a pratyekabuddha, nor the stage of a bodhisattva, nor the stage of a Tathāgata. He does not perceive the stage of a cakravartin king, nor the stage of a Śakra, nor the stage of a Brahmā, nor the stage of a Mahābrahmā, nor the stage of a Maheśvara, nor the stage of a Paranirmitavaśavartin, nor the stage of a Vaśavartin, nor the stage of a Nirmāṇarati, nor the stage of a Tuṣita, nor the stage of a Yāma, nor the stage of a Trāyastriṃśa, nor the stage of a Cāturmahārājika, nor the stage of a human being, nor the stage of a god, nor the stage of a nāga, nor the stage of a yakṣa, nor the stage of a gandharva, nor the stage of an asura, nor the stage of a garuḍa, nor the stage of a kiṃnara, nor the stage of a mahoraga, nor the stage of a preta, nor the stage of a piśāca, nor the stage of a kumbhāṇḍa, nor the stage of a pūtana, nor the stage of a kaṭapūtana, nor the stage of an amanuṣya, nor the stage of a bhūta, nor the stage of a kṛtya, nor the stage of a vetāla, nor the stage of a rākṣasa, nor the stage of a yakṣiṇī, nor the stage of a nāginī, nor the stage of a piśācinī, nor the stage of a kumbhāṇḍinī, nor the stage of a pūtanā, nor the stage of a kaṭapūtanā, nor the stage of an amanuṣyinī, nor the stage of a bhūtinī, nor the stage of a kṛtyā, nor the stage of a vetālī, nor the stage of a rākṣasī. He does not perceive the stage of the hells, nor the stage of animals, nor the stage of the world of Yama. He does not perceive the stage of the form realm, nor the stage of the formless realm. He does not perceive the stage of the past, nor the stage of the future, nor the stage of the present. He does not perceive the stage of birth, nor the stage of old age, nor the stage of sickness, nor the stage of death, nor the stage of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. He does not perceive the stage of the conditioned, nor the stage of the unconditioned. He does not perceive the stage of saṃsāra, nor the stage of nirvāṇa. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma. Because he does not perceive any dharma and does not apprehend any dharma, he is called a ‘bodhisattva. [124,ii] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor apprehend any dharma, how does he go forth toward omniscience? How does he train in the six perfections? How does he enter into the emptinesses? How does he enter into the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? How does he enter into the dhāraṇī-doors? How does he enter into the ten stages? How does he enter into the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? How does he enter into the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How does he enter into the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the bodhisattva? How does he enter into the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma. Because he does not perceive any dharma and does not apprehend any dharma, he goes forth toward omniscience. Because he does not perceive any dharma and does not apprehend any dharma, he trains in the six perfections. Because he does not perceive any dharma and does not apprehend any dharma, he enters into the emptinesses. Because he does not perceive any dharma and does not apprehend any dharma, he enters into the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Because he does not perceive any dharma and does not apprehend any dharma, he enters into the dhāraṇī-do

Now, if only the specific location (*deśaviśe�șa*) is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and not its qualifier (*tadviśeṣaṇa*), then there would be no absence of its definition [of perception], because of the contact with that which is sought. In that case, however, meditative practitioners (*dhyāyin*) who know things such as the "unborn" (*anutpanna*) would not have cognition based on a location and so forth. Furthermore, if perceptual knowledge arises from contact with only one part of the object of knowledge, then everyone would be a seer of everything (*sarvapratyakṣadarśin*), since it is possible for something to be a qualifier in some way for everything in contact with the senses. Moreover, even in the absence of the definition of inference, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [inferential] memory being perception, because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the cause there, not the existence of the object; for [memory] occurs even when the object is absent. This is the same in the other case [of perception]. Since the merit born of yoga (*yogajadharma*) is the cause, there is no proof for the utility of the object there; for it is accepted that the yogic perception arises in all cases—whether the object is present or absent, hidden or unhidden, and whether it is present or not present. By asserting that the basis is a present location and so forth only in the absence of a mark (*liṅga*) and so on, you would be rejecting the convergence (*saṃplava*) of the means of knowledge. And by imagining [perception] to be distinct from inference and so on, you contradict the Sūtra; for you imagine a non-Sūtra [definition] to refute inference and the rest. If you say it is not a non-Sūtra because it refutes inference and so on, then the explanation of the term "non-verbalizable" (*avyapadeśya*) for the purpose of excluding verbal testimony (*śabda*) would be improper. Furthermore, the acceptance of six kinds of contact and the inclusion of the sense organ (*indriya*) for the purpose of excluding inference and so on would be self-contradictory. Therefore, the mind (*manas*) is dependent on the senses, marks, and so forth. If everything were complete within the scope of ordinary means of knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*), then even one who operates with ordinary means of knowledge would possess complete knowledge, and thus there would be no distinction for one who claims to have supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*). If it is clear manifestation (*spaṣṭāvabhāsa*) that constitutes [supramundane] knowledge, then the [ordinary] means of knowledge has no utility therein. If it is certainty (*niścaya*), that is equal to the validity of the other [means of knowledge] as well. For one who sees everything through perception, there is no further desire (*nairākāṅkṣya*) regarding any object, but this is not the case for the other. If even what is not perceived is complete because it has been measured by another means of knowledge, what else would he desire? There is no desire for another means of knowledge, since that desire is for the sake of establishing the object of knowledge (*prameya*). If it is for the sake of establishing the object again, no; for it has already been established repeatedly by the previous [means]. And there is no reason to require the establishment of what is already established. If there is the existence of another means, that would simply be a desire for another means. If it is a particular pleasure that is achieved through the vision born of the previous means of knowledge, then another means is useless. And due to the existence of another means, one who desires to know again might desire to know what has already been seen by others; for there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since perception consists of certainty while inference and so on do not. In that case, the desire arises precisely from the fact that it is not yet established. For that which is deviant and lacks certainty is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Perception is capable of manifesting [an object] through contact, whereas inference and so on are not. If it is said that movement and so forth are required as the instrument of contact, but not as the instrument of the valid cognition itself—since the cognition is already established and contact is the cause of the manifestation once the cognition exists—then the point at issue is that perception has an object not in contact, and thus it is not sufficient for the cessation of desire. Therefore, there is indeed no distinction between the ordinary and the supramundane cognizers. Because inference and so on have universals (*sāmānya*) as their objects, the ordinary cognizer has a state of desiring more, because they do not ascertain the specific nature restricted to each individual object. If you say that even the supramundane cognizer has no such desire because they ascertain time and form, then there is no distinction. If, then, the ordinary means of knowledge has an incomplete object, the supramundane one—which consists of mental cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*)—is dependent on that [cultivation] and cannot take that [incomplete object] as its domain. It has already been explained that the external mind has no independence. Therefore, the claim that "everything is the object of the mind" is mere prattle. Moreover—
Existing only as a false appearance, it is not perception in any other sense;
for neither succession nor simultaneity can be conceived, nor can an object of cognition be defined.

[129,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. This is called the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom become one who has set out correctly? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor forms, nor eye-consciousness; nor the ear, nor sounds, nor ear-consciousness; nor the nose, nor odors, nor nose-consciousness; nor the tongue, nor tastes, nor tongue-consciousness; nor the body, nor tangibles, nor body-consciousness; nor the mind, nor mental phenomena, nor mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm. He does not perceive the conditioned, nor the unconditioned. He does not perceive the past, nor the future, nor the present. He does not perceive the stream-enterer, nor the fruit of stream-entry; nor the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; nor the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; nor the arhat, nor the fruit of arhatship; nor the pratyekabuddha, nor the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood; nor the bodhisattva, nor the fruit of bodhisattvahood; nor the Tathāgata, nor the fruit of Tathāgatahood. He does not perceive even nirvāṇa as real. Subhūti, this is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom and has set out correctly. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, how does he generate the thought of awakening? How does he train in the six perfections? How does he enter the stages? How does he purify the Buddha-fields? How does he mature sentient beings? How does he turn the wheel of Dharma? How does he demonstrate the great parinirvāṇa? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that he generates the thought of awakening. It is because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that he trains in the six perfections. It is because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that he enters the stages. It is because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that he purifies the Buddha-fields. It is because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that he matures sentient beings. It is because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that he turns the wheel of Dharma. It is because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that he demonstrates the great parinirvāṇa. Subhūti, this is the way a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom.”

Other means of knowledge (*māna*) have as their domain objects that exist across the three periods of time, whereas perception has only the present as its object. In this regard, for one who perceives [the present] as having a non-present nature, it is false cognition, because everything is not of that [non-present] nature. However, for one who perceives it according to its actual state, it is not perception, because perception lacks the capacity to have past or future objects. Alternatively, one must necessarily provide a single definition for this manifold variety of perception; otherwise, there would either be no justification for designating it a distinct means of knowledge, or one would have to accept other means of knowledge [for perception], since there is no purpose for such a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*). Furthermore, people in common usage apply the word "perception" even to certain things with different characteristics, so that [definition] does not apply to supramundane perception. In that case, being "born from the sense-organ" (*akṣaja*) is not the definition, as it overextends (*ativyāpti*) to the mind (*manas*). Therefore, the definition is: "being produced from an object in contact with a sense-organ. As it has been said: "Because it arises through the power of the object, [perception] is produced from the contact of the sense-organ and the object; thus, it is 'contact with the existent' (*satsaṃprayoga*). Since the mind is a sense-organ, this definition extends to the cognition of pleasure and so forth; and by specifying "produced by the power of the object," it excludes inference and the rest. Moreover, since subtle, remote, and obstructed objects lack the capacity to produce cognition, the possibility of a perception whose object is everything is not established. If it is argued that the definition of perception is "freedom from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), then what is this "conceptual construction"? If it is a cognition appearing as a word (*śabdābhāsa*), then auditory cognition would not be perception. Or, if it is an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpa-saṃsarga-yogya-pratibhāsa*), [then the same fault follows].

[132,i] Even in the case of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*), there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*). Now, if it is argued that there is direct perception because of the association of one thing with another thing (*vastvantara*) within the object, this is not so, because a universal as a distinct entity (*vastvantara*) is not admitted. [133] Or, if it is argued that there is direct perception due to the association with a verbal designation (*abhidhāna*), then this would apply only to one who has not mastered verbal designations.

[133,i] Now, if it is argued that perception is the cognition of mere form, free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), by superimposing [form] onto that which is formless, then the knowledge of yogins or others regarding things not yet born or already passed away would not be perception; for the form appearing in cognition does not exist in those [objects]. Or, if it did exist, it would follow that they are present.

Because it imitates a superimposed form, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) occurs therein; for there is no superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of knowledge other than the imitation of a non-existent form. [Objection: But surely, since superimposition must have a basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the cognition of one thing as having the form of another is conceptual construction. [Reply: In that case, the cognition of hair and so forth by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimiraka*), being without a basis, would be perception (*pratyakṣa*). Or, if some basis is asserted for that, then the cognition "a sky-flower" would be a non-conceptual perception. Furthermore, the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) as having the form of a universal would not be of the nature of superimposition, just as in self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*). [Objection: If conceptual construction is merely the imagination of a form, then cognition regarding the past, the unborn, and so forth, would not be free from conceptual construction. [Reply: If conceptual construction is the cognition of a universal-form with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), then that is perception; however, with respect to a universal, it is erroneous (*bhrānta*).

What, then, is this "error"? If it is the state of having an unreal object (*asadarthatā*), then that would apply equally to the cognition of an omniscient being. If, on the other hand, it is the state of having an absolutely unreal object, then cognitions such as those of one with ophthalmia or dreams would be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If "non-erroneousness" consists in correspondence with causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsaṃvāditva*), then if pleasure and pain, or their attainment and avoidance, were dependent solely on the object, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a cognition incapable of prompting action or avoidance would be erroneous. If it is the production of successive cognitions [that constitutes non-error], then momentary consciousness would possess that quality [of being non-erroneous]. Therefore, error is the apprehension of identity in that which lacks that nature. And thus, the cognition of an omniscient being is neither free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) nor non-erroneous; it does not conform to the definition of direct perception. However, in this case, the cognition proceeding in the form of experience (*anubhavākāra*) does indeed conform [to the definition]. As it has been said: "Even mental [cognition] proceeding in the form of experience is direct perception. Now, what is this "form of experience"? If it is the nature of being conscious (*bodhātmakatā*), then all cognition is so. If it is the appearance of another individual instance (*vyaktyantarā'vabhāsatā*), then even the first encounter with an indistinct yellow object due to distance and so forth would not be direct perception. If it is the cognition of something not distant, internal, or obscured, then there is the undesirable consequence that the cognition of universals (*sāmānya*) would be direct perception. If it is thought that the "form of experience" is the manifestation of what is proximate and present, and that the vision of yogins and Tathāgatas regarding all objects is of such a nature—that is incorrect. Because the previous faults have not been avoided. Furthermore, because one sees what is not as it is in that which is of such a nature, it is merely false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), like the vision of one with ophthalmia. Direct perception does not become otherwise [than non-erroneous]; its characteristic is being produced by the capacity of the sense organ and the object. Otherwise, for what reason would the vision of hair and such, produced by the affliction of ophthalmia and so forth, not be confused? All direct perception indeed manifests what is not proximate. This is because there is a difference in time between the object and the cognition, due to their relationship as cause and effect. What, then, is this that appears? It is the form of the cognition itself. For at this moment, no one is a perceiver of even a single part of the whole through direct perception. There is no loss of the perception of the object, because the observation of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) occurs precisely through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the experience within the form of the cognition. How can there be a determination of one thing when there is the experience of another? Due to the deep-rootedness of ignorance (*avidyā*), characterized by a chronic obsession with grasping objects since beginningless time. Well then, long live omniscience, which is a massive case of the epilepsy of ignorance! Better is the lesser ignorance of being a perceiver of only one part. Moreover, even by mere convention, only a single part could be direct perception. Since the state of being an object (*grāhyatva*) is the state of being a cause capable of imparting its form to the cognition, not everything [is perceived]; because that [other part] is not a cause, either spatially or temporally, due to its non-proximity. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of everyone being omniscient. Or else, is the cognition only of a present form, or also of past and future forms? In the former case, since everything is not of such a nature, it is false. In the latter case, it is not direct perception because it proceeds by constructing forms such as the past and so forth. Or else, everything would be known at the time of cognition either as having a present nature or as existing in that state [past/future]. In the former, there is falsity. In the latter, not everything is direct perception, because states other than the present are not being directly perceived. Furthermore, it is not possible to comprehend everything sequentially due to infinity. For there is no finality (*pariniṣṭhā*) to a knowable object that arises and is devoid of prior and posterior limits. Nor is it simultaneous, for the same reason of infinity. If the extent is not determined, there is no distinction between the comprehension of the whole and a single part. But surely, even without determining the extent, one perceives everything simultaneously by way of its form? This is not sound. For if the extent is not determined, neither "everything" nor "a single part" is determined, because neither is excluded. In the case of a collection of many substances, the comprehension of the whole occurs only through the determination of the extent, and that is possible only in the finite, not in the infinite. And the comprehension of the knowable depends on the form of the cognition. And there is no infinity among the forms residing in a single cognition occurring simultaneously, because they are all present. For those whose space and time are uninterrupted—those unborn, those already passed, and those present—are infinite when considered together; and the past is infinite because its prior limit is not delimited, and even if it were delimited, [the future] is before it. But the present things are delimited by both limits; as many as have arisen, so many they are—how can there be infinity? Therefore, there is no single cognition with infinite forms, nor are there infinite cognitions simultaneously. Furthermore, what is this "all" that the knower of it is "omniscient"? It is not the objects taken individually, nor even a few of them accompanied by others and governed by some commonality. Such a state is not possible in the case of infinite things. If it is argued that "all" means the primary infinite itself—that is not so. Even if there is infinity for those belonging to one or the other temporal limit, they are not "all"; whereas those delimited by neither prior nor posterior are "all. Moreover, if "all" is indeed the infinite, its determination is impossible. To explain: if all individuals are determined, then they are just that many and not infinite. If they are not determined, they are infinite; and if they are infinite, how can there be their determination? If, then, "all" refers to objects delimited by the three times—that is not so, because there is no such delimitation among them, as they are no different from a single part. Therefore, since there is no mode of existence other than sequential or simultaneous, and since cognition is pervaded by those two, cognition is impossible when those two are absent. And because of the absence of objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Furthermore, since inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by direct perception, they too have no causal efficacy regarding the "all," because there is no grasping of a relation either directly or indirectly through direct perception. For the same reason, there is no verbal testimony (*śabda*), because the meaning of a sentence is like the meaning of a word qualified by another word. There is no presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there is no observation of something that cannot be accounted for in its absence. There is no comparison (*upamāna*), because its object is similarity. There is no non-existence (*abhāva*), because its object is absence. Just as with direct perception, sequentiality and simultaneity are not possible for the other means of knowledge, and their objects of knowledge cannot be defined. Thus, first of all, there is non-establishment [of omniscience]. Cognition also [is not established].
[145,i] Since all that is invisible is not the object of the cognition of other sense faculties,
for this very reason, the effect of the knowledge of an omniscient being is not established.

[145,ii] First of all, for one who does not perceive supersensible objects (*anindriyadṛś*), even a subsequent consciousness is not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). For this very reason, it is not inferable (*anumeya*); because that [consciousness] is unestablished, its effect is also unestablished. Now, an objection is raised: "The attainment of the limit (*kāṣṭhāprāpti*) of degrees of excellence has been observed in the case of measurable things (*parimāṇa*); and knowledge is such a thing characterized by degrees of excellence. Therefore, when it reaches its limit somewhere, it must have everything as its object. To this it is replied: If "limit" (*kāṣṭhā*) means a boundary (*avadhi*), then let it be so; however, it must be something beyond which nothing further is possible.
There is an inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to products that are effects, and due to qualities such as heaviness (gurutva) and so forth.

[146,i] The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are these four? They are: 1) the self-nature of attachment (*abhiniveśa-svabhāva*), 2) the self-nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), 3) the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and 4) the self-nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of attachment? It refers to the grasping at the characteristics of objects through the habitual tendencies of beginningless ignorance, which gives rise to the manifestation of the triple world. This is called the self-nature of attachment. What is the self-nature of conceptualization? It refers to the various names, signs, and appearances that are falsely imagined by ordinary beings based on the characteristics of objects; this is called the self-nature of conceptualization. What is the self-nature of dependent origination? It refers to the arising of all phenomena from causes and conditions, devoid of the characteristics of a creator or a self; this is called the self-nature of dependent origination. What is the self-nature of perfected reality? It refers to the non-duality of the self-nature of conceptualization and the self-nature of dependent origination, being eternally free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence; this is called the self-nature of perfected reality. These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of self-nature."

If that which beyond which nothing exists is the "limit" (*kāṣṭhā*), let it be granted that there is an attainment of that [limit]. However, by that alone, the establishment of omniscience (*sarvaviṣayatva*) is not achieved; rather, there would only be possession of a vast number of objects. Just as a terrestrial globe, compared to other terrestrial objects, occupies a much larger space of ether, yet this is not all-pervasiveness (*sarvavyāpitā*). Now, if [the limit] is defined as that beyond which nothing further is possible, then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to produced substances (*kāryadravya*). For even jars and the like, despite their excellence, do not possess an excellence of dimension beyond which no further possibility exists, because that would entail the impossibility of any other [space] and because a single [substance] would occupy all space. Nor is it correct to say that this [excellence] is a property of qualities (*guṇadharma*), because such a state is impossible for qualities such as heaviness (*garima*) residing therein; for there is no production of a single effect by all things possessing heaviness simultaneously. Furthermore, the reaching of near or distant places occurs through specific efforts, as seen in humans, wind, deer, lions, and birds; yet there is no excellence of that effort beyond which no further state is possible, because space (*nabhas*) is infinite. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence that some who have attained the unsurpassed [height] would fall, since effort would be unsurpassed only through the attainment of every destination without exception. Since space is infinite, how could there be unsurpassedness for that [effort]? Therefore, there is a deviation with respect to effort itself as a unique quality, or with respect to the quality of intellect (*buddhi*). That [state] is not the limit of merit (*dharma*) which results in sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); likewise, it is not so for the merit that generates sovereignty, because the sovereignty of God (*Īśvara*) is not the fruit of merit. Moreover, due to the non-contact with afflictions, karma, its ripening, and latent dispositions (*āśaya*), there would be the consequence of multiple sovereignties, which would result in a contradiction of sovereignty. Furthermore—
If space were limited, it would not be impossible for it to reach another state;
however, because its nature is infinite, these [elements] do not possess the quality of finite measurement.

If it is argued that [God is omniscient] because of His infinity (*anantatva*), what is this "infinity"? It is being unlimited (*aparicchinna*). But is this not simply the absence of measurement? In that case, this very absence constitutes His measurement. By asserting such a pinnacle of attainment for the knowledge of God, you reveal Your own ignorance. This is like the rising of a *vetāla* (vampire) during a rite for peace. [Objection: Then, His omniscience follows simply from His being the agent (*kartṛ*) of all effects. For potters and other agents are those who know the material cause (*upādāna*), the instruments (*upakaraṇa*), the recipient (*sampradāna*), and the purpose (*prayojana*). Since God is the agent of all effects, He must know the material causes and so forth of every effect; and thus, He is omniscient. [Reply: Do these agents know all the instruments of their respective effects without exception, or only some? First, they do not know all the instruments without exception, because they do not know the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Nor do they know the specific recipient or purpose, since there can be many such recipients and purposes; knowing only that much does not establish omniscience. Furthermore, children, the insane, and others are not knowers of the purpose and so forth of all effects. If agency is something yet to be proven (*sādhya*), how can it establish omniscience without a logical reason (*hetu*) that already includes that omniscience within itself?
Is it not already established that those things possessing arrangement and so forth must be preceded by an intelligent agent?
This is news.
[155,i] Although everything possessing arrangement and so forth has an intelligent cause,
how can there be a single cause for the well-known arrangement and the rest?

Even though trees, mountains, oceans, and so forth differ from the arrangement of palaces and other such structures built with prior deliberation, if [you argue that they are caused by an intelligent agent] merely because of the commonality of being "arrangements," then—given that we observe creations involving subsequent suffering, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of favoring others—it would follow that the existence of a mere conscious being is established, even if the absence of a purpose has already been refuted. But how could its unity be established? For jars, chariots, and the like are not preceded by a single intelligent mind. If you say that they are so [preceded by a single mind] because they are preceded by Īśvara, that is a point yet to be proven (*sādhya*). Since an arrangement is invariably concomitant with mere consciousness, and since this is observed in some cases, you might claim it is so in other cases as well. If this is your argument, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the example and the point to be proven. If everything were to be proven, there would be no example. Furthermore, if [the world] had two makers, then since jars and the like have two makers, the world and so forth would likewise have two; this leads to the consequence of an infinite regress of Īśvaras. For this very reason, the second inference is invalid. In that case, let the first inference also be abandoned, for the infinite regress remains equal. Now, if you say that jars and the like do not have two supervisors, but rather everything has a single supervisor, then the omniscience [of that supervisor] is not established. We see in the world that parts such as the wheels of a chariot are produced by various craftsmen, yet they generally function as mutual causes and effects. Thus, while the parts of a chariot are seen to be preceded by a single carpenter, you conclude that the world must also be preceded by a single creator. This is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*), because we also observe things preceded by multiple craftsmen.
An effect is not inferred when it is rejected by the absence of a cause;
nor is the cause mere consciousness, for such a view is logically untenable.

[159,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the field of generosity as real, nor does he perceive the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real? How is it that he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real? How is it that he does not perceive the eye as real, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real? How is it that he does not perceive forms as real, nor sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real? How is it that he does not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real? How is it that he does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real? How is it that he does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real? How is it that he does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real? How is it that he does not perceive the field of generosity as real, nor the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real? How is it that he does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as real? How is it that he does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor the state of a tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one as real? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. He does not perceive the eye as real because the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real because the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. He does not perceive forms as real because forms are empty of the intrinsic nature of forms; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real because sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are empty of the intrinsic nature of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as real because eye-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness; he does not perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real because ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. He does not perceive eye-contact as real because eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-contact; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real because ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty of the intrinsic nature of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real because that which arises from eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from eye-contact; he does not perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real because that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. He does not perceive the element of earth as real because the element of earth is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of earth; he does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real because the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness. He does not perceive the field of generosity as real because the field of generosity is empty of the intrinsic nature of the field of generosity; he does not perceive the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real because the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom are empty of the intrinsic nature of the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real because the fruit of a stream-enterer is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of a stream-enterer; he does not perceive the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as real because the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, and an arhat are empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, and an arhat. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real because the fruit of a pratyekabuddha is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha; he does not perceive the state of a tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one as real because the state of a tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one is empty of the intrinsic nature of the state of a tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; if the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye, and if the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; if forms are empty of the intrinsic nature of forms, and if sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are empty of the intrinsic nature of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; if eye-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness, and if ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; if eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-contact, and if ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty of the intrinsic nature of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact; if that which arises from eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from eye-contact, and if that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact; if the element of earth is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of earth, and if the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness; if the field of generosity is empty of the intrinsic nature of the field of generosity, and if the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom are empty

Indeed, in the absence of the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*), neither the connection with a body and senses for that [being], nor intellect, nor sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) is possible; thus, the acceptance of such [a being] contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For when there is no cause, the effect cannot arise. Or, if it were to arise, its inference would not be from its configuration (*saṃniveśa*). If, on the other hand, it were preceded by the latent deposit of karma, then knowledge of that [deposited karma] would have to come from another source. [Objection: But surely, precisely because there is no effect in the absence of a cause, there is an inference of that [cause]? Otherwise, even a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) would not be possible. Or rather, a distinction must be stated as to why a refutation is not a proof (*sādhana*). [Reply: It is said: By perception, configurations that are distinct and not preceded by a conscious intention (*apratyayapūrva*) would be non-causes of that [consciousness]. And in this way, intellect (*buddhi*) is not to be inferred, because inference proceeds from similarity to what is perceived (*dṛṣṭasālakṣaṇya*). Furthermore, although they are equal [in being logical], a refutation functions through mere opposition, whereas a proof establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) only when its counter-arguments have been eliminated. Moreover, it is not mere intellect that is the cause of configuration, but rather *prekṣā*—which consists of deliberation and determination regarding the purpose of the arrangement. And that [deliberation] is not possible there [in a creator], because of the absence of any purpose for oneself or for others. [Objection: Let there be no omniscient director; let him be known as one who knows Dharma (*dharmajña*). For it has been stated that a restriction of the objects of the eyes and other senses is not determined by their form (*rūpa*). However, if the restriction is temporal, then when they are present, it is not contradictory for the eyes and other senses to have as their object that which possesses excellence (*atiśaya*). And if they are absolutely non-present, then absolute non-existence follows, like a sky-flower; this has already been stated. In that context, Dharma is the meaning of "one should act," since sacrifice and other such objects are accepted as being Dharma. If it is argued that it is imperceptible because it is something to be produced (*utpādya*), then let it be so for that which is yet to be produced. [Reply: Even when produced, it is Dharma by its own nature, but its status as a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhana*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). What, then, is this "being a means to the highest good"? If it is a potency (*śakti*), and that is beyond the senses, then it has been said here: the restriction of the objects of the senses is not well-established either by their number or by their magnitude. Or, if you say it is because that [Dharma] is non-existent at that time, we reply: because the highest good occurs at a different time. Let it be so, otherwise its status as Dharma would be lost. But the means to the highest good, while present, is not outside the range of the senses. [Objection: Practitioners desire the knowledge of Dharma prior to performance. Thus, the future [Dharma] is not an object of the senses. [Reply: We do not say that Dharma is perceptible to the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), but rather to a teacher who possesses excellence. And that excellence may be innate, like the vastness of space, or born of other instructions, or dependent on action; thus there is no fault.
It is said:
The capacity of an action that perishes in a single moment is unequal in duration to its fruit; therefore, they say that this [capacity] is not perceived by direct perception.

[163,ii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; and if another person were to take up even a single verse from this Dharma-discourse and teach it to others, the latter would generate a far greater accumulation of merit than the former."

An excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by the agent—which gains its origin from the karma that is dissolving; which undergoes various intermediate states brought about by preceding and succeeding factors; which attains a distinction of transformation through space, time, and so forth; and which transcends even the immediate sequence of the karma—is said to be the means for accomplishing the fruit of a karma that occurs at a later time. This [excellence] does not exist at the time of the karma. Even though it exists at its own time, because the karma has already passed away, it is not perceived as being connected to the karma. As it has been said: "At that time, it does not exist in the form of a means for the fruit. At the time of the karma, this [excellence] is yet to come (*bhāvitva*), and at the time of its [own] manifestation, the karma is absent. How, then, can the karma be a means when it is inherent in something other than itself? Because it is produced by that [karma]. There is no rule that only that which is inherent in the same substrate (*svasamavāyin*) can be a means. That [excellence], which is to be inferred from the effect, is properly located only where it is capable of producing the effect; its power (*śakti*) belongs there because it was instilled by that [karma]. Nor is the status of karma as a means merely figurative (*aupacārika*), for it is established in exactly the same way in the case of firewood (*kāṣṭha*) and the like. [Objection: Some maintain that such a thing does not exist, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). Nor is presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) a valid means of proof, because it would undermine the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) regarding the connection with the fruit. For if that [connection] were unestablished, it would attain establishment only through the injunction and presumptive testimony; thus, it would become the very cause of the presumption. Otherwise, if the connection between karma and fruit were established otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence of having to resort to presumptive testimony. Once that [connection] is established, what else could be required to postulate that [apūrva]? For [the injunction] is not independent. Even if it were dependent, if it required another entity while the connection between sacrifice and fruit is already understood, how could that [entity] be understood if the former is not understood? A sentence-meaning cannot consist of a word-meaning that has not been understood. If it requires another means of knowledge, its independence (*anapekṣatva*) would be contradicted. Furthermore, either the heard sentence is untenable due to its dependence, like the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," because of the need to supply an unstated direction; or the meaning is untenable. In the former case, one must assume a supplement to the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). But there is no such untenability, since the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" is complete and lacks a supplement. If one were to say "having performed the apūrva," it would follow that the apūrva arises prior to the sacrifice. If one says "having performed the apūrva by means of the sacrifice," there is a double use of the verb *yaj* and the aforementioned fault remains. In the latter case, if it is untenable because it is heard [in the text], the same alternative applies. It is incorrect to say that the apūrva is postulated for the sake of establishing what is heard, on the grounds that it is untenable in its current nature.
It is said:
Instruction consists of an injunction for the sake of one who is to be enjoined, concerning an action not yet undertaken.
It is well known that [this rule] does not apply even in the case of a preceptor, a physician, and so forth, when they are present constantly.

[169,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the eye as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive forms as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the earth element as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive ignorance as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive generosity as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive the state of a tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened buddha as a basis for apprehension. Why is that? Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they are not to be cultivated. Because they are not to be cultivated, they do not increase. Because they do not increase, they do not decrease. Because they do not increase or decrease, they are neither produced nor extinguished. Because they are neither produced nor extinguished, they are neither defiled nor purified. Because they are neither defiled nor purified, they are beyond conceptual proliferation. Because they are beyond conceptual proliferation, they are equal. Because they are equal, they are the same. Because they are the same, they are the dharma-realm. Because they are the dharma-realm, they are the sphere of activity of the Tathāgatas. Because they are the sphere of activity of the Tathāgatas, they are the ultimate limit. Because they are the ultimate limit, they are the suchness. Because they are the suchness, they are the unchanging suchness. Because they are the unchanging suchness, they are the true suchness. Because they are the true suchness, they are the non-false suchness. Because they are the non-false suchness, they are the unaltered suchness. Because they are the unaltered suchness, they are the reality-limit. Because they are the reality-limit, they are the dharma-nature. Because they are the dharma-nature, they are the fixed nature of dharmas. Because they are the fixed nature of dharmas, they are the self-nature of dharmas. Because they are the self-nature of dharmas, they are the emptiness of dharmas. Because they are the emptiness of dharmas, they are the signlessness of dharmas. Because they are the signlessness of dharmas, they are the wishlessness of dharmas. Because they are the wishlessness of dharmas, they are the uneffort of dharmas. Because they are the uneffort of dharmas, they are the unconditioned of dharmas. Because they are the unconditioned of dharmas, they are the unarisen of dharmas. Because they are the unarisen of dharmas, they are the unproduced of dharmas. Because they are the unproduced of dharmas, they are the non-existence of dharmas. Because they are the non-existence of dharmas, they are the non-coming of dharmas. Because they are the non-coming of dharmas, they are the non-going of dharmas. Because they are the non-going of dharmas, they are the non-abiding of dharmas. Because they are the non-abiding of dharmas, they are the non-dwelling of dharmas. Because they are the non-dwelling of dharmas, they are the non-apprehensibility of dharmas. Because they are the non-apprehensibility of dharmas, they are the non-manifestation of dharmas. Because they are the non-manifestation of dharmas, they are the non-perception of dharmas. Because they are the non-perception of dharmas, they are the non-conceptualization of dharmas. Because they are the non-conceptualization of dharmas, they are the non-distinction of dharmas. Because they are the non-distinction of dharmas, they are the equality of dharmas. Because they are the equality of dharmas, they are the sameness of dharmas. Because they are the sameness of dharmas, they are the one taste of dharmas. Because they are the one taste of dharmas, they are the non-duality of dharmas. Because they are the non-duality of dharmas, they are the non-multiplicity of dharmas. Because they are the non-multiplicity of dharmas, they are the non-differentiation of dharmas. Because they are the non-differentiation of dharmas, they are the non-separation of dharmas. Because they are the non-separation of dharmas, they are the non-attachment of dharmas. Because they are the non-attachment of dharmas, they are the non-obstruction of dharmas. Because they are the non-obstruction of dharmas, they are the non-hindrance of dharmas. Because they are the non-hindrance of dharmas, they are the non-grasping of dharmas. Because they are the non-grasping of dharmas, they are the non-clinging of dharmas. Because they are the non-clinging of dharmas, they are the non-identifying of dharmas. Because they are the non-identifying of dharmas, they are the non-appropriating of dharmas. Because they are the non-appropriating of dharmas, they are the non-owning of dharmas. Because they are the non-owning of dharmas, they are the non-possession of dharmas. Because they are the non-possession of dharmas, they are the non-attachment of dharmas. Because they are the non-attachment of dharmas, they are the non-bondage of dharmas. Because they are the non-bondage of dharmas, they are the non-liberation of dharmas. Because they are the non-liberation of dharmas, they are the non-arising of dharmas. Because they are the non-arising of dharmas, they are the non-ceasing of dharmas. Because they are the non-ceasing of dharmas, they are the non-defilement of dharmas. Because they are the non-defilement of dharmas, they are the non-purification of dharmas. Because they are the non-purification of dharmas, they are the non-increase of dharmas. Because they are the non-increase of dharmas, they are the non-decrease of dharmas. Because they are the non-decrease of dharmas, they are the non-production of dharmas. Because they are the non-production of dharmas, they are the non-extinction of dharmas. Because they are the non-extinction of dharmas, they are the non-coming of dharmas. Because they are the non-coming of dharmas, they are the non-going of dharmas. Because they are the non-going of dharmas, they are the non-abiding of dharmas. Because they are the non-abiding of dharmas, they are the non-dwelling of dharmas. Because they are the non-dwelling of dharmas, they are the non-apprehensibility of dharmas. Because they are the non-apprehensibility of dharmas, they are the non-manifestation of dharmas. Because they are the non-manifestation of dharmas, they are the non-perception of dharmas

Although commands (*ājñā*) and requests (*abhyarthanā*) are inappropriate in the Veda, instruction (*upadeśa*) is appropriate. That too, like them, is recognized in the world as a fourth [type of speech] consisting of instigation (*preraṇā*). For instance: a command and a request direct the action toward an object while disregarding the fruit for the person being enjoined (*niyojya*), whereas instruction has the welfare of the person being enjoined as its purpose. As for permission (*anujñā*), even if it is sometimes like this, it is not "instruction" because it concerns a person who is already engaged in activity. The wise define instruction as the instigation of one who has not yet begun activity toward an action that serves the purpose of the person being enjoined. Indeed, there is no perception of "instruction" in such cases as "Drive the cow," "Teach the boy," or "Do as you please. Nor is there a perception of a command and so forth in such cases as "One should practice begging" or "One suffering from fever should eat wholesome food. Furthermore, this [instruction] is mostly recognized in the world among human compositions—such as treatises on desire and wealth—as being unstained by commands and the like; for example, in the words of cowherds and others intent on describing a path: "One should go by this way. For a subordinate person does not issue a command regarding an action for his own sake, nor does he request or grant permission to one who is not yet engaged. Precisely for this reason, it is called "instruction. Since it is perceived as distinct from commands and the rest, its knowledge is termed "instruction," and thus it is shown by the word "instruction" as being distinct from those. Let it be distinct from those; but what is it? Has it not been stated that "instruction" is the utterance of a specific word? If that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of even an unlearned person engaging in activity. It is said in reply:
He [the author] states the specific means for the pure human goal—
that human goal which is desired by a person, at whatever time, and by whatever means.

[171,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving, nor does he perceive the donor, nor does he perceive the recipient. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness; he does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness; he does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness; he does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness; he does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness; he does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the aggregates, nor does he perceive the elements, nor does he perceive the sense-fields; he does not perceive conditioned phenomena, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena; he does not perceive the past, nor does he perceive the future, nor does he perceive the present. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the emptiness of internal phenomena, nor does he perceive the emptiness of external phenomena, nor does he perceive the emptiness of both internal and external phenomena; he does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness, nor does he perceive great emptiness, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the ultimate, nor does he perceive the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, nor does he perceive the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, nor does he perceive absolute emptiness, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, nor does he perceive the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor does he perceive the emptiness of nature, nor does he perceive the emptiness of all phenomena, nor does he perceive the emptiness of self-characteristics, nor does he perceive the emptiness of non-existence, nor does he perceive the emptiness of existence, nor does he perceive the emptiness of non-attainment, nor does he perceive the emptiness of non-dharmas, nor does he perceive the emptiness of dharmas and non-dharmas.
