[173,i] The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are these four? They are: the self-nature of imagined characteristics (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha (*tathāgatagarbha-svabhāva*). Mahāmati said: "What is the self-nature of imagined characteristics? The Blessed One replied: "It is the attachment to names and signs as being real entities, based on the false discrimination of what has no external object. Mahāmati asked: "What is the self-nature of dependent origination? The Blessed One replied: "It is the manifestation of various appearances arising from the habit-energy of false discrimination, which, though lacking any external objective support, appears as such through the power of interdependence. Mahāmati asked: "What is the self-nature of perfected reality? The Blessed One replied: "It is the non-duality of the two natures—the imagined and the dependent—realized through the cessation of false discrimination, and it is the state of being eternally free from the duality of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati asked: "What is the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha? The Blessed One replied: "It is the storehouse of all seeds, which is the basis for both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; it is the womb of the Tathāgatas, which, when purified of the defilements of adventitious afflictions, becomes the Dharmakāya."

For *pravartanā* (incitement) is a certain excellence (*atiśaya*) of an entity capable of producing activity, which is designated as "operation" (*vyāpāra*). And that is simply the fact that [the action] is a necessary means (*apekṣitopāyatā*) for actions; for no one engages in them without first understanding them to be such. Even the engagement resulting from commands and the like depends in some way upon having recourse to a necessary basis; otherwise, it would not exist. Now, one might object: engagement follows from the cognition that "this must be done. For how could one who understands it thus fail to engage? Who could give an answer to one who, having perceived gold, says it is clay? But what is the meaning of "this must be done"? None at all. It is *pratibhā* (intuition). What, then, is this? It is an intelligence (*prajñā*) conducive to the comprehension of an action delimited by specific means. For when intuition has the action as its object, there arises the cognition of the action, and that is the cause of engagement. That which is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) is not a factor in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), for doubt and error are likewise [not factors]. Indeed, even when an object is understood through perception and other means, one does not engage in it without the emergence of a specific intuition (*pratibhābheda*) such as "this must be done by him in this manner," for it is there that the function of the means of knowledge reaches completion. For the world acts toward its duties (*itikartavyatā*) with intuition as its eye. What, then, is the cause of this intuition? It is the Word (*śabda*). In that regard, for those who are proficient, it is either the direct [cognition] or the latent impression (*bhāvanā*) of the Word; for children and others, whose linguistic practice is based on words not yet well-established, it is the beginningless latent impression of the Word. Otherwise, the initial arrangement of the organs of action and so forth would be impossible. As it has been said: [The text continues with the cited verse: *...saṃskāraḥ saiva ca pratibhā...* etc.
The initial arrangement of the instruments, the upward movement of the vital breath,

Furthermore, even for word-meanings that are perceived separately, how could they be synthesized? One who is devoid of deliberation (*vicāra*) and has not reflected upon their prior capacity brings about a connection (*upaśleṣa*) when there arises an intuition (*pratibhāsa*) of a capacity previously experienced, because that [connection] exists for the sake of that [intuition], and would be absent otherwise. Even among the wise, regarding birds whose means of cognition are difficult to discern and whose distinctions depend on specific accents, it is the intuition—following the prior *śabdabhāvanā* (the latent impression of words) and possessing the operation of the present word—that is the cause of activity, not the knowledge of the means, since there is an absence of both instruction and repeated observation. Furthermore, the acquisition of specific food by members of that species would not be based on a first cognition if the means of pleasure were unknown. Likewise, the engagement in activities such as swimming by those of a single species, whose differences in intuition are manifested by differences in genus, occurs without known means; and there is the activity of passion (*rāga*) and the like, as well as the activity of hatred (*dveṣa*) among those who are eternally opposed. Therefore, the elders have shown that it is not merely the desired means that is the cause of activity, but rather intuition (*pratibhā*). [181,ii] Is this intuition (*pratibhā*) indeed possessed of an objective referent (*ālambana*), or not? If it is possessed of an objective referent, then that very thing must be understood as the basis for engagement (*pravṛtti-nibandhana*), and not anything other than the state of being the means to the desired goal (*īhita-upāyatā*).
But knowledge that is without an objective support is simply untenable.
Because its characteristic is the function of illuminating the object of knowledge;
and since there would be no possibility of linguistic convention due to the absence of objects, it would follow that it functions independently of those conventions.

[192,i] But surely, it may be argued, action associated with causal factors (*kāraka*) is indeed accepted as the objective basis (*ālambana*). No; for even when there is a manifestation (*prakhyā*) produced by words that cause the cessation of that [action], since it is the same [in both cases], there would follow the undesirable consequence of non-activity due to a difference in intuition (*pratibhā*) arising from words joined with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.

[192, ii] Is it not the case that there exists no speech which neither prompts to action nor restrains from it? For such would be useless; for the function of a sentence culminates in a sense of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*). How then are the Vedāntas, which describe existing things, and other non-worldly (extraordinary) statements to be understood? Because they differ in their sense of what is to be done, as they have as their objects the comprehension of engagement or desisting from action. Indeed, every sense of what is to be done possesses a distinction. In the Vedāntas, for instance, the sense of what is to be done is the comprehension of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). In the world, however, the culmination of a statement is that "this treasure or the like is to be comprehended here. <ed_193>

This is not sound. Since comprehension arises from the word, the word has no further operation regarding that [comprehension], just as in the case of the cognition of the connection between an action and its fruit. Furthermore, if the certainty [of truth] also comes from the word, it has already been produced; if it comes from another source, then the word lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Nor is there "intentionality toward the meaning" (*arthaparatā*), because the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) does not have a visible purpose, like a ritual action, according to the maxim: "The meaning of a sentence is not distinct [from the injunction]. Otherwise, it would follow that only those texts containing injunctions possess intended meaning. Moreover, an injunction is not sought merely for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*), since knowledge has the manifestation of the object of knowledge as its result, and no other result is admitted. Furthermore, because an injunction is intent upon action, the actual existence of the thing itself is not intended; thus, while one might infer performance for the sake of comprehending that [thing], there would be no realization of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). Therefore, the injunction heard in such cases is unintended, because it is already eternally established.

Now, it may be argued that that which is devoid of an injunction (*vidhi*), being merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and possessing expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*), cannot attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). But what is this "restativeness"? Is it the state of having an object already apprehended by another means of knowledge, or is it the state of having an existent fact as its object? If it is the state of having an object already apprehended by another means of knowledge, then even a non-human (Vedic) text that is devoid of an injunction and does not possess such [an already-apprehended] character would not be a restatement. If, on the other hand, it is the state of having an existent fact as its object, then how can there be dependence (*sāpekṣatā*)? For while worldly speech concerning existent facts—such as statements regarding the drinking of medicinal herbs—is seen to be dependent because its scope is an object already apprehended by another means of knowledge, worldly injunctions are likewise so; thus, even that which possesses an injunction would have to be dependent. If, however, it is argued that it does not depend [on others] due to its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*), then non-human origin is useless even for that [existent fact]. Or, if it is argued that the dependence of an existent fact arises from the possibility of other means of knowledge, but not so for an injunction, then since that [other means of knowledge] is impossible regarding the object of an injunction, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even worldly [injunctions] would be independent.

Since the application (*viniyoga*) depends upon human intellect, it is dependent upon that [intellect] even in the case of non-human (authorless) speech. Furthermore, that [application] is not only independent of other cognitions; it is also not the object of other means of knowledge (*māna*). If it were so, then the authorless word would be independent because of this lack of dependence; for the cause of dependence is not the impossibility of other means of knowledge. Rather, the state of being authored by a person (*pauruṣeyatā*) is the cause of dependence. Even in worldly speech which culminates in an injunction (*niyoga*), there is dependence due to its being dependent [on other means], and thus there is no possibility of another means of knowledge [being required]. Moreover, if dependence were to result from the possibility of a mutual scope between perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), then their status as valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) would be lost due to such dependence. Therefore, a statement is dependent either because its activity is preceded by the desire to express what is perceived through another means of knowledge, or because it possesses an injunction (*vidhi*) while the other does not. Since neither of these two conditions applies to Vedic [speech], both are independent; this is well-established. Consequently, even for the sake of establishing validity, there is no requirement for the intention to express an injunction.

[197,i] But surely, this knowledge whose object is the reality of the Self is enjoined as something entirely different from that which arises from words. For the nature of Brahman is not to be fully comprehended through verbal knowledge. Since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of a sentence has as its meaning the connection between word-meanings, and the reality of the Self is the cessation of the entire manifold of difference (*bhedaprapañca*), how can it be the object of such [verbal] knowledge? Therefore, a different kind of knowledge—one whose essence is the manifestation of the non-dual reality (*advaitatattva*) and in which all delineations of limitations have dissolved—is enjoined as distinct from verbal knowledge.

This is a trivial matter. Indeed, the portion consisting of the fruit (*phala*) is not within the scope of an injunction (*vidhi*). The manifestation of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is free from phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), is itself the fruit; nothing other than that is desired. If you say it is "liberation" (*mokṣa*), it is because there is no difference between the two. For the manifestation of the reality of the Self as possessing phenomenal proliferation is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), whereas the manifestation of the Self as free from phenomenal proliferation is liberation—namely, abiding in one's own Self. Otherwise, because it would be something produced (*kārya*), it would not be liberation. Furthermore, the cause of bondage is the phenomenal world of karma and so forth, which is ignorance (*avidyā*); its eradication is indeed knowledge (*vidyā*) alone. Moreover, if Brahman is in no way whatsoever the object of verbal cognition, how can an injunction to know it be understood? The definition of knowledge is established by way of its object, and that [Brahman] defines it as something already established (*siddha*). Its establishment would have to occur through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since there is an absence of any other means. If that [Brahman] were also not an object, then due to its non-establishment, there would be no comprehension of a specific knowledge, and thus no comprehension of the injunction. If, on the other hand, it is somehow an object, then there is no independence from verbal cognition. And since the statement would be intent upon the duty of comprehension (*pratipatti-kartavyatā*), it has been said that such a nature [of Brahman] would not be the meaning of the scripture (*āgama*). Nor is it the case that the meaning is merely implied (*ārtha-artha*), for comprehension is possible even through superimposition (*adhyāropa*). Therefore, the true nature of reality (*vastutattva*) is not revealed by entering into the sphere of an injunction (*niyoga*). For in that regard, the word lacks authority (*prāmāṇya*). Thus, since its authority is established through independence, it is incorrect to say that the Veda is capable of making known even that which is an existing entity (*bhūta*) devoid of connection to an action (*kārya*). If the meaning of the Veda consists solely of what is to be done (*kārya-rūpa*), then how are the Mantras, Arthavādas, and the Upaniṣads [to be explained]? Because the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) itself makes known the meaning that is an existing entity and so forth. How so? By making known the meaning that is an action (*kārya-artha*), it also makes known the existing entity and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that it is the production of a continuous stream of verbal cognitions [that constitutes the result], because that has as its fruit a pure and clear knowledge in which all delineations of difference have been withdrawn. Even in this case, there is no realization of the nature of the Self; and since the excellence of knowledge is well known to be dependent upon practice, it cannot be the purpose of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*). Therefore, specific injunctions pertain to rituals with perceptible results. As for the reality of the Self, it is understood from the Upanishadic statements independently of any other injunction. Enough, then, with this dispute with the teachers.

Or rather, let it be that the comprehension of the reality of the Self occurs by way of an injunction regarding the duty of practice; for it has been stated that the majority of worldly statements are merely descriptive accounts of what has already come to be.

[201,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to be liberated from their suffering. Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “If, Śāriputra, there be any sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should perceive that all five aggregates are empty of self and what belongs to a self. Then, Śāriputra, by perceiving that form is emptiness and emptiness is form, and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—that is, by perceiving that consciousness is emptiness and emptiness is consciousness—then, Śāriputra, all suffering is transcended. Furthermore, Śāriputra, because there is no birth and no cessation, no defilement and no purity, and no decrease and no increase, therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind; no form, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touch, and no object of mind; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment, and because there is no attainment, one dwells in the realization of the fruit of an Arhat. Therefore, Śāriputra, all the Buddhas of the three times, relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which relieves all suffering and is true, not false; therefore, proclaim the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā, saying: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With these words, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, as well as the entire assembly and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and faithfully upheld what the Buddha had taught. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā train? The Blessed One said to the Venerable Subhūti: “A son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā should thus train: they should perceive that form is empty of form, and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—they should perceive that consciousness is empty of consciousness. Why is this? Because form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. Likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Why is this? Because Subhūti, all dharmas are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, Subhūti, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind; no form, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touch, and no object of mind; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment, and because there is no attainment, one dwells in the realization of the fruit of an Arhat. Therefore, Subhūti, all the Buddhas of the three times, relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which relieves all suffering and is true, not false; therefore, proclaim the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā, saying: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. [202,iii] At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it is wonderful how the Tathāgata has spoken of the profound Prajñāpāramitā. Blessed One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and give them as a gift to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and if another person were to hear and uphold even a single verse of this profound Prajñāpāramitā, the latter would generate far more merit than the former. Why is this? Because, Blessed One, the Buddhas of the three times, relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Subhūti: “So it is, so it is. Subhūti, it is as you say. Is it not the case that futility has been stated here? This [charge of futility] applies equally even to an injunction for comprehension (*pratipatti-vidhi*), because the comprehension of an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*) does not differ from [the result of an injunction]. If you argue that it is precisely the comprehension of the self as it truly is (*aviparītātma-pratipatti*) [that constitutes the result], then that is equally present even when a narrative of an existing fact (*bhūtākhyāna*) reaches its conclusion. Let it be, then, that all speech culminates in action (*pravṛtti-paryavasāyitva*); even an existing fact is told so that one may act elsewhere or toward that very fact itself, since otherwise there would be no purpose. No, for the cessation of curiosity (*kutūhala-nivṛtti*) is also a purpose. To illustrate: questions are seen among the curious regarding things that are neither to be avoided nor sought after, such as the names of kings or the deeds of those in distant lands. And the words of those who know these things are intended solely for the satisfaction of curiosity. Descriptions of forests and the like in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, which are devoid of both engagement and withdrawal, culminate in the existing fact and serve as causes of pleasure through their mere form; and narratives intended to produce pleasure are for the sake of generating delight in the listener, not for the sake of inducing engagement or withdrawal. Enough of this over-elaboration.

Just as for young children, birds, and others, a remote sound serves as the cause for intuition (*pratibhā*) through the persistence of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), why is it not accepted that knowledge of the means (*upāyajñāna*) functions in the same way, by way of engagement and withdrawal? Furthermore, specific types of birth and other factors serve as awakeners of the cultivation of knowledge of the means, just as they do for the cultivation of verbal impressions (*śabdabhāvanā*).

[203,i] But surely, since the objective support (*ālambana*) of intuition (*pratibhā*) is not established by way of its own nature, it is defined only through the form of verbal cognition. And yet, no presently existing word exists. Therefore, one must resort to mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This is not sound. For this non-establishment of the objective support of intuition is stated either because it is not present, or because it lacks a unitary nature due to being a composite of multiple objects. That same [non-establishment] applies equally to the word as well. For even that [word], consisting of a composite of past phonemes (*varṇa*), does not exist as a single entity. It has already been stated that this is because there is no perception of difference and there is a perception of non-difference. <ed_204>

[204,i] But surely, in the case of such things, you have accepted that the cognition of a non-different entity consists of a single word-essence. For indeed, among non-entities—such as conjunction (*saṃsarga*), a collection (*samūha*), or absolute non-existence (*atyantāsattva*)—or among entities that are conjoined but possess diverse natures, the appearance of a single entity is not possible without the mediation of a single word-essence, whether by way of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), transformation (*pariṇāma*), or manifestation (*vivarta*). No; for it is established otherwise. First, conjunction, which is characterized as the meaning of a sentence, has action as its primary element with the factors of action (*kāraka*) as subordinate, and involves a conjunction of elements whose primary status is unequal.

Even a collection (*samūha*) cannot exist without a single cause for its manifestation among the members of that collection; in that case, the single illumination (*ekaprakāśa*) serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Even things such as a hare’s horn, when conceptualized (*utprekṣyamāṇa*) in the form of an object perceived in another class of things, manifest as having the nature of a real entity (*vastvātmaka*). Otherwise, there would be no unity of sentence (*ekavākyatā*) in what is understood from a single sentence. Nor is there a difference in the word (*śabdabheda*) therein, because there is no difference in its form (*rūpa*). If it is argued that the difference [of the word] arises from a difference in meaning (*arthabheda*), how could something perceived in one way be otherwise? If it is argued that this is due to the inference of a difference in meaning, then the difference or non-difference of meanings would be understood first, and only afterwards the difference or non-difference of words; thus, the appearance of oneness in objects is not caused by the proximity of the word. Furthermore, there would be no distinction between a "collection" and a "single word. Moreover, for one who does not know the word "collection," the manifestation of that [oneness] would not occur at a distance. And in the phrase "non-existence is a word," since there is a cognition of the word "existence" (*bhāva*), the intended meaning would be lost. As for the theories of illusory transformation (*vivarta*) or evolution (*pariṇāma*), since everything is one, intermediate oneness could not be the basis for a single word. Furthermore, the distinction between real and unreal entities (*vastvavastuvibhāga*) would not exist. If it is argued that even though the illusory transformation of the word is the same, this distinction is based on something else—no, it is based on the illusory transformation of the word itself. For in cases such as a hare’s horn or a fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*), there is the determination of the form of a real entity. And much has already been exerted by our own colleagues [on this point], so enough of this digression. Therefore, being the means to what is desired (*īpsitopāyatā*) is the cause for the agent's engagement.

[211,i] Activity arises solely from the cognition that something ought to be done (*karttavyatā*), not from the fact that it is a means to a desired end (*īpsitopāyatā*). For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-activity even with regard to obligatory rites (*nitya*); or, if they were means to a desired end, their status as obligatory would be contradicted.
It is said: Through the preceding words, there is conventional usage that does not depend upon etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).
What could be the specific cause for the seed [of the teaching] being present in the hearing of the meaning?

[211,iii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive generosity as real, nor does he perceive morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, or Arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real. Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive any dharma as real."

What, then, is this cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the word? Is it the seed for the knowledge of the word itself, having the word as its object, or is it the seed for the knowledge of the meaning expressed by the word? If it were the former—having the word as its object—there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to those very words from previous lives whose impressions (*saṃskāra*) of memory have not perished; furthermore, linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) would not be required in that case. If it were the latter—[the seed] for the meaning expressed by the word—even so, if the former [seed] exists, the same objection applies. Or perhaps it is only this [latter kind]. A specific reason must be stated why, when proficiency, practice, and attention toward the relation between word and meaning are equal, the seed of cultivation pertains only to the meaning and not to the word or the relation. Death, suffering, or the intervention of another birth might destroy the seeds of cultivation regarding the word and the relation, but not regarding meanings. And if there were a persistence of cultivation even regarding those [words and relations], then those born deaf in another life would describe types of forms and sounds experienced in that life as if they had been experienced in a previous birth. Furthermore, since a newborn child experiences joy, fear, and grief due to the connection with memories of what was practiced previously, it follows that some cultivations persist and not all. This is because the child’s behavior is like that of one who is proficient [in language].
Be that as it may, however—
Because it depends upon what has already been established, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for that [ultimate reality] itself;
rather, the operation of inferential marks (liṅga) and scriptural statements (vākya) occurs with respect to what is established in a general sense, and then toward the specific [particular].

[213,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who were practicing the practice of the Dharma and, having beheld them, addressed them as follows: "Sisters, what is the Dharma that you are practicing? They replied: "Venerable sir, we are practicing the Dharma of the emptiness of all phenomena. He said: "Sisters, what is the emptiness of all phenomena? They replied: "Venerable sir, it is the emptiness of form, the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of formations, and the emptiness of consciousness; it is the emptiness of the eye, the emptiness of the ear, the emptiness of the nose, the emptiness of the tongue, the emptiness of the body, and the emptiness of the mind; it is the emptiness of forms, the emptiness of sounds, the emptiness of odors, the emptiness of tastes, the emptiness of tangibles, and the emptiness of mental objects; it is the emptiness of the element of earth, the emptiness of the element of water, the emptiness of the element of fire, the emptiness of the element of wind, the emptiness of the element of space, and the emptiness of the element of consciousness; it is the emptiness of the faculty of faith, the emptiness of the faculty of vigor, the emptiness of the faculty of mindfulness, the emptiness of the faculty of concentration, and the emptiness of the faculty of wisdom; it is the emptiness of the power of faith, the emptiness of the power of vigor, the emptiness of the power of mindfulness, the emptiness of the power of concentration, and the emptiness of the power of wisdom; it is the emptiness of the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the emptiness of the factor of enlightenment of discernment of phenomena, the emptiness of the factor of enlightenment of vigor, the emptiness of the factor of enlightenment of joy, the emptiness of the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the emptiness of the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the emptiness of the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; it is the emptiness of the noble truth of suffering, the emptiness of the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the emptiness of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the emptiness of the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; it is the emptiness of the aggregate of morality, the emptiness of the aggregate of concentration, the emptiness of the aggregate of wisdom, the emptiness of the aggregate of liberation, and the emptiness of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; it is the emptiness of the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the emptiness of the ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless emptiness, the emptiness of the non-dispersal emptiness, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature in other things. [214,i] He said: "Sisters, what is the emptiness of form? They replied: "Venerable sir, form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; it is not by means of another form that form is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of form is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of form. Sisters, what is the emptiness of feeling? Feeling is empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling; it is not by means of another feeling that feeling is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of feeling is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of feeling. Sisters, what is the emptiness of perception? Perception is empty of the intrinsic nature of perception; it is not by means of another perception that perception is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of perception is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of perception. Sisters, what is the emptiness of formations? Formations are empty of the intrinsic nature of formations; they are not by means of another formation that formations are empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of formations is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of formations. Sisters, what is the emptiness of consciousness? Consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness; it is not by means of another consciousness that consciousness is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of consciousness is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of consciousness. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the eye? The eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye; it is not by means of another eye that the eye is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the eye is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the eye. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the ear? The ear is empty of the intrinsic nature of the ear; it is not by means of another ear that the ear is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the ear is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the ear. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the nose? The nose is empty of the intrinsic nature of the nose; it is not by means of another nose that the nose is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the nose is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the nose. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the tongue? The tongue is empty of the intrinsic nature of the tongue; it is not by means of another tongue that the tongue is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the tongue is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the tongue. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the body? The body is empty of the intrinsic nature of the body; it is not by means of another body that the body is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the body is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the body. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the mind? The mind is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind; it is not by means of another mind that the mind is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the mind. Sisters, what is the emptiness of forms? Forms are empty of the intrinsic nature of forms; they are not by means of another form that forms are empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of forms is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of forms. Sisters, what is the emptiness of sounds? Sounds are empty of the intrinsic nature of sounds; they are not by means of another sound that sounds are empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of sounds is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of sounds. Sisters, what is the emptiness of odors? Odors are empty of the intrinsic nature of odors; they are not by means of another odor that odors are empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of odors is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of odors. Sisters, what is the emptiness of tastes? Tastes are empty of the intrinsic nature of tastes; they are not by means of another taste that tastes are empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of tastes is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of tastes. Sisters, what is the emptiness of tangibles? Tangibles are empty of the intrinsic nature of tangibles; they are not by means of another tangible that tangibles are empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of tangibles is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of tangibles. Sisters, what is the emptiness of mental objects? Mental objects are empty of the intrinsic nature of mental objects; they are not by means of another mental object that mental objects are empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of mental objects is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of mental objects. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the element of earth? The element of earth is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of earth; it is not by means of another element of earth that the element of earth is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the element of earth is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the element of earth. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the element of water? The element of water is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of water; it is not by means of another element of water that the element of water is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the element of water is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the element of water. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the element of fire? The element of fire is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of fire; it is not by means of another element of fire that the element of fire is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the element of fire is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the element of fire. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the element of wind? The element of wind is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of wind; it is not by means of another element of wind that the element of wind is empty. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of the element of wind is itself empty. This is called the emptiness of the element of wind. Sisters, what is the emptiness of the element of space? The element of space is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of space; it is not by means of another element of space that the element of space is empty.

First of all, cognition produced from a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [Supreme Self], because it depends on prior establishment due to its origin in consciousness. Nor is it produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because it depends on a cognition of its cause. Nor is it produced from a logical mark or a sentence; for since these two depend on the established existence of a general form (*sāmānyarūpa*), they cannot bring about the comprehension of a sentence-meaning involving an unestablished category if they only penetrate a specific [particular]. Thus, when there is a dependence on a means of knowledge based on the establishment of a general form, and that is absent, there is a lack of validity. And just as it is so in this life, so too was it required in previous and even earlier lives; thus, there is a total absence of a means of knowledge [for it]. In that case, one might argue that this is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on beginningless verbal impressions (*śabdavāsanā*), but that has already been refuted above.
Moreover—

For the worldly understanding is that what is a means to the agent's desired end is "to be done," whereas in the opposite case it is "not to be done"; therefore, [the status of being dharma or adharma] resides in those respective objects.

Indeed, that causal condition which follows after a particular object is the objective domain (*viṣaya*) of that cognition, just as white is the domain of the cognition of "white. For ordinary people, the cognitions of "what ought to be done" and "what ought not to be done" follow respectively from the state of being a required means and its opposite. Therefore, it is understood that these two are the domains of those [cognitions].

Therefore, even "duty" (*kartavyatā*) is nothing other than being the means to what the agent desires. As it has been said: "The fruit of that which is to be done is happiness. How, then, can there be eternality or duty in the case of the obligatory rites (*nitya*)? It is through the performance of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) according to one's capacity. For instance, if the son and so forth were the desired object, then the eternality of the means would be destroyed, because that desire is non-eternal; in that case, the phrase "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīvam*) would be meaningless. Nor is it meaningful as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*), since the purpose is already established.

Now, it might be thought that for everyone, at all times, every desired result will arise as the removal of accumulated evil (durita). This would indeed be the case regarding its permanence, but not by virtue of the verbal testimony (śabda), but rather by virtue of the result. For, since the result is always desired, its necessity is real by virtue of that [desire]. The verbal testimony, however, merely indicates the cognition of the means to that which is always desired. In that regard, if there were no operation of the word, then—just as in the case of the *arthakṛcchra* and other such rites—there would be no requirement to perform all the constituent parts (*aṅga*), because otherwise the result would not occur. If the permanence were based on the word itself, then because it is impossible for it to be both complete in its parts and always occurring, the phrase "as far as one is able" (*yathā śaknuyāt*) becomes appropriate. Otherwise, since the scriptural injunction of the parts (*aṅgāmnāya*) would be non-optional, the rule "whoever [performs it]" would apply, as in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others. Indeed, in the *Viśvajit*, not everyone is eligible (*adhikārin*), such as the lame and others; nor is the incidental result (*ānuṣaṅgika*) what is desired, due to a lack of evidence. Furthermore, since the sin of omission is destroyed even by the non-performance of a prohibited act, it is more reasonable to assume the result [of the permanent rite] through the force of memory (*smṛti*) and the remainder of the scriptural statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). Moreover, from memory, the meaning of that [result] is understood again. And just as a sin is incurred by the performance of what is prohibited and must not be done, it is logical that a sin is incurred by the non-performance of what is enjoined and must be done, because such an injunction is possible. Since one engages in the means to a desired end out of a desire [for it], and not out of fear of sin, the kind of engagement [required for a permanent rite] is not the same [as that for a desired end]. Therefore, the assumption of a sin in non-performance is based on the fact that these [permanent rites] are not the means to a desired end, are permanent, possess a result, and are to be performed according to one’s ability. Consequently, permanent rites are not the means to a desired end, nor are they permanent [in the sense of being optional]. And engagement in them occurs because of the assumption of a sin in non-performance. Furthermore, since action is of the nature of suffering, [the result arises] from the destruction of the *pāpa* (evil) which is incidental and opposed to the task. And since the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is something to be accomplished, and since—as in the case of "the Agnihotra"—it can serve as the object of designation and thus be modified, there is no contradiction in the use of the instrumental case. But this is trivial. For it is as follows: [The text continues with the refutation of the opponent's view.]
Since it is heard in scripture that "as long as one lives" refers to the means for attaining the eternal that is eternally beneficial,
the constituent parts [of the path] must therefore be practiced according to one's capacity; otherwise, not all of them need be performed.

[220,ii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is a stream-enterer, the person who is a once-returner, the person who is a non-returner, and the person who is an arhat. Thus it was said. How many fruits of the spiritual life (śrāmaṇyaphala) are there? There are four fruits of the spiritual life. What four? They are: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. Among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of being a stream-enterer. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of being a once-returner. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of being a non-returner. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of being an arhat. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the abandonment of three fetters, namely: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and adherence to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa). What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the attenuation of two fetters, namely: sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill will (vyāpāda). What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the complete abandonment of five lower fetters, namely: the view of a self-identity, doubt, adherence to rules and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the complete abandonment of all defilements (āsrava) together with their residual impressions (vāsanā). Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the attainment of the first fruit of the spiritual life. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the attainment of the second fruit of the spiritual life. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the attainment of the third fruit of the spiritual life. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the attainment of the fourth fruit of the spiritual life. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the realization of the first stage of the noble path. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the realization of the second stage of the noble path. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the realization of the third stage of the noble path. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the realization of the fourth stage of the noble path. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having entered the stream. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of returning only once more to this world. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of not returning again to this world. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having exhausted all outflows and attained liberation. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of being irreversible from final enlightenment. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having only one more birth remaining. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, upon rebirth, with effort, without effort, or in the higher realms. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of being an arhat who has destroyed the taints, who has lived the holy life, and who has done what was to be done. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the states of misery and hell. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having only one more human birth remaining. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of attaining parinirvāṇa in the realm of form (rūpadhātu). What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of attaining parinirvāṇa in the realm of formlessness (ārūpyadhātu). Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having abandoned the five lower fetters. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having abandoned the five higher fetters. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having abandoned the five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having abandoned all fetters. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four floods (ogha). What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four bonds (bandhana). What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four graspings (upādāna). What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all graspings. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four attachments (āsava). What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four perversions (viparyāsa). What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four nutriments (āhāra). What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all nutriments. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna). What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa). What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda). What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all bases of psychic power. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four meditative concentrations (dhyāna). What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four immeasurables (apramāṇa). What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti). What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all formless attainments. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four truths (satya). What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid). What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four dharmas of a great man (mahāpuruṣadharma). What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all dharmas of a great man. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four fruits of the spiritual life. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four paths (mārga). What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four fruits of the path. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all fruits of the path. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa). What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four bases of mindfulness. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four right efforts. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all right efforts. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four dhyānas. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four immeasurables. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four formless attainments. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all formless attainments. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four truths. What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four analytical knowledges. What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the state of having transcended the four dharmas of a great man. What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the state of having transcended all dharmas of a great man. Furthermore, among these, what is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the state of having transcended the four fruits of the spiritual

First of all, even if [the rite] is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), there is no contradiction with its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), because it is precisely that which is eternally desired—the removal of evil—that is conceived as the goal to be accomplished. Regarding pleasure or its cause, one may at times remain indifferent; however, for one who is always repelled by suffering and its causes, there is a constant desire for their cessation. Furthermore, for one who seeks what is beneficial, there is indeed an effort toward the destruction of obstacles. Therefore, the destruction of sin, being based on what is desired, is always sought after. Since the fruit of obligatory rites is eternal, as understood from the word "throughout life" (*yāvajjīvam*), there is no contradiction with their obligatory nature. For if the goal were non-eternal, that [obligatory nature] would be violated. And the performance according to one's capacity (*yathāśaktyupasaṃhāra*) follows precisely from this obligatoriness, because the performance of the rite without missing any parts is impossible in the case of an obligatory duty. Moreover, this is not a real (*vāstavam*) obligatoriness. Those who maintain that there is a fruit do not recite the word "throughout life," nor do they study a word specifying a particular fruit; rather, having understood the obligatoriness from the scriptural hearing of "throughout life," they sometimes infer a distinction in the fruit and a distinction in the application through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). If the goal were non-eternal and the application were complete in all parts, the obligatoriness understood from the word "throughout life" would be untenable. Indeed, the word "throughout life" does not apply to an obligatoriness that consists merely of a means to something desired at some time, nor to one consisting of a means performed with all parts complete. And the distinction in the fruit imagined due to obligatoriness does not contradict that very [obligatoriness]. How then was obligatoriness stated to be due to being a means to what is eternally desired? It was stated that there is no obstruction to that very [obligation] understood from the scripture, which is obtained through the power of the words themselves, by performing according to one's capacity and by means of the *tantra* (simultaneous performance). Therefore, no other means of knowledge (*māna*) needs to be sought for these two. And how can this be the obligatoriness of the rite if it is defined as being a means to what is eternally desired? Is it not established simply from the word itself, since there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in its non-performance due to its constant practice? This is not so. If its obligatoriness comes from the word alone, what is the purpose of postulating a transgression in its non-performance? Since activity is already established by the word alone, and it has been stated that a word is not a cause of activity by way of being a producer (*kāraka*), but rather a communicator (*jñāpaka*), then if it prompts constant practice by communicating the transgression in non-performance, it would have to be real. Therefore, such various manifestations arise for those whose understanding of the nature of injunctions (*vidhi*) is unsettled. In the case of the *Kṛcchra* and *Viśvajit* sacrifices, although they are always means to what is desired by everyone, the performance of all parts is required because of the absence of the words "always" or "for everyone. Now, if there is a fruit, performance according to capacity is not possible, because of the consequence that the fruit would be absent due to deficiency (*vaiguṇya*). What is this deficiency? It is the loss of the status of being the object of the injunction (*codanārthatva*). If that is so, it is not a deficiency, because even when performed according to capacity with all parts, it remains the object of the injunction. Or, if it were not the object of the injunction, then even if the capacity were fruitless, there would still be a performance of all parts, because otherwise the purpose of the injunction would never be fulfilled. In that case, since there is no goal to be accomplished apart from the act itself, there is no requirement for parts. It follows that the rite would be without parts, because the rite is known as a means [to an end]. If it is argued that the act (*kriyā*), though its nature is known as something to be enjoined, requires parts for the fulfillment of the injunction’s purpose, then there would be the consequence of including all parts. If it is argued that for verbs expressing their meaning, capacity (*śakti*) is a cooperative factor, and thus capacity is the object of the injunction due to the hearing of "throughout life"—then for those who maintain there is a fruit, that [capacity] cannot be forcibly denied. Furthermore, what is this form of the injunction? If it is the name "Darśapūrṇamāsa," then since that is understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there would be an absence of those [parts] not produced by it. If it is something else, that is not so, because it is a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥsādhanatva*). As it has been said: "For their status as means to the highest good is always understood from the Veda," and "This is their instruction: 'This is the means to that. Nor is there the status of being a cause of transgression in non-performance, because it is impossible for a non-existent thing to be a cause.
And since the status of being a goal to be accomplished (sādhya) is equal, there is no logical inconsistency regarding the *prayāja* offerings and other such rites.

[225,ii] For that which is useless with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*) or its effect (*kārya*) cannot be a constituent part (*aṅga*). Furthermore, there is no such application (*prayukti*) for this kind of thing. Nor can there be engagement in action because of the suffering involved due to the incidental destruction of sin, if it were not sanctioned by scripture (*aśāstrīyatva*), like climbing upon a heated stone and so forth. Moreover, if it were caused by sin, human effort (*puruṣakāra*) would be rendered futile; if it were not caused by that [sin], there would be no destruction [of the sin]. However, there is no fault if the ripening [of the karma] occurs through a scriptural means. [226,i]

If, then, even in a rite possessing a fruit there is no requirement to include all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), the same would apply to optional rites (*kāmya*) as well. If it is argued that this is so only in the other case because of the scriptural injunction for "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), then let it be the same here as well because of the scriptural injunction for "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*). Just as it is impossible to perform [the rite] for the duration of one's life without omitting some parts, so too it is not possible for every person desiring heaven to perform it in its entirety; rather, at whatever time and in whatever manner a person is able to perform them, at that time and in that manner, he shall include only those many parts he is capable of. For while the injunction for "one desiring heaven" refers to anyone who seeks the result and thus accords with the specific [capacity], when there is an expectation of capacity, the injunction for the auxiliary parts is not contradicted. Therefore, unlike the obligatory (*nitya*) rite, the injunction for "one desiring heaven" does not serve as a reason for adhering to a specific [limited] performance.

Now, it might be thought: "In order not to obstruct the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*), the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga-vidhi*)—which apply without distinction—should indeed be restricted according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*). This is the same even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*); for the scriptural injunction 'as long as one lives' (*yāvajjīva*) has no other possible application. In that context, the injunction for one desiring [a specific result] (*evaṃkāma-śruti*) is perfectly consistent even with respect to one capable of performing all the subsidiaries. Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the performance of the principal rite (*aṅgin*) follows those subsidiaries according to the maxim of the 'one who eats from a bronze bowl' (*kāṃsyabhojinī-nyāya*). True, the restriction of the scope of the injunction for one desiring heaven has been shown to be free of contradiction. However, when there is a conflict between the subordinate and the principal, following the principal is preferable, as is seen in the world. For example, in the command, "Feed the Brahmins with food prepared with various kinds of utensils," the restriction regarding the Brahmins is not altered by the arrangement of utensils according to one's capacity. Likewise, the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries do not possess absolute dependence [on the principal]. Therefore, even in optional rites (*kāmya*), let it be simply "as far as one is able" (*yathā śaknuyāt*), and not "whenever one is able" (*yo yadā śaknuyāt*), since there is no difference [in the nature of the requirement]. This is not sound. It would result in a discrepancy in the single injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) and lead to the postulation of multiple performances. Furthermore, since there is no usage of words in isolation, and because there is no contradiction with the specific scriptural statement (*viśeṣa-śruti*), that very injunction of performance would both enjoin and not enjoin the performance of that very subsidiary. Moreover, there would be the fault of excessive conceptualization (*kalpanā-gaurava*), as the performance would differ according to the difference in capacity. And since it is universally established that when a word is connected with another word, it possesses a specific referent (*viśeṣa-paratva*), there is never a ground for an unjustified assumption. If it is argued, "Then let it be the same way even in the case of the obligatory rite: 'as long as one lives, whenever one is able,'" [we reply: if you say the term 'as long as' (*yāvat*) is untenable, then how could it apply to rites with indefinite causes? Furthermore, there would be the consequence of having to perform the oblation (*homa*) continuously. If you say this is not so because of the adherence to the mention of a specific time, then alas! Even the scriptural injunction 'as long as one lives,' while conforming to the injunctions of the subsidiaries, must follow its connection with capacity; thus, due to the conformity with the subsidiary injunctions, it should be "whenever [one is able]."

[230,i] The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, when a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters, he is one who will attain parinirvāṇa in the interval. "What is meant by 'attaining parinirvāṇa in the interval'? Ānanda, suppose a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters; having arisen in a certain realm of rebirth, while still in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), he attains parinirvāṇa. This is called 'attaining parinirvāṇa in the interval. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu who has abandoned the five lower fetters, having arisen in a certain realm of rebirth, attains parinirvāṇa upon reaching the place of birth. This is called 'attaining parinirvāṇa upon arrival' (*upahacca-parinibbāyī*). Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu who has abandoned the five lower fetters, having arisen in a certain realm of rebirth, attains parinirvāṇa after having traversed half the life-span. This is called 'attaining parinirvāṇa with effort' (*sasankhāra-parinibbāyī*). Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu who has abandoned the five lower fetters, having arisen in a certain realm of rebirth, attains parinirvāṇa without effort. Ānanda, a bhikṣu who has abandoned the five lower fetters, having arisen in a certain realm of rebirth, goes from that realm to another, and from that realm to yet another, proceeding successively upward until he reaches the Akaniṣṭha heaven, where he attains parinirvāṇa. This is called 'one who goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! Now, it might be thought: even while living, one is entitled (*adhikriyate*) to perform a ritual only when it possesses its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), for there is no injunction (*vidhāna*) for a performance devoid of parts. However, the performance (*prayoga*) of one who is so entitled does not cease until the entitlement itself ends, nor is it restricted by the presence of all parts; rather, it proceeds as far as possible, because that performance is dependent upon the entitlement. Furthermore, this does not apply to optional (*kāmya*) rites. This is because the entitlement for an optional rite culminates in the effect (*kārya*), whereas the entitlement for a conditional (*naimittika*) rite culminates in the performance. Since the effect depends on the means (*sādhana*), and since the status of being a means is understood only as long as all parts are present, the accomplishment of the effect occurs only through the inclusion of all parts. Objection: In both cases, it is the entitlement alone that must be fulfilled. True. But in one case (the conditional) it terminates with the occurrence of the occasion (*nimitta*), while in the other (the optional) it terminates with the attainment of the fruit (*phala*). In the case where it terminates with the occasion, if the person possessing the occasion fails to perform the rite, they merely transgress their entitlement; thus, the performance proceeds as far as possible. In the case where it terminates with the fruit, however, if there is a deficiency in the parts, the fruit is not produced. Since the desire for the fruit is the cause of the entitlement, it ceases; and because the entitlement no longer exists, there is no fault of "transgressing the entitlement," and thus the performance is not undertaken in an arbitrary manner. Therefore, there is no requirement for constant performance (*sātatyena prayoga*), and while there is an inclusion of parts according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*) in obligatory (*nitya*) rites, this is not the case for optional ones. Thus, everything is logically consistent.

[234,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the eye as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive forms as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the earth element as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the realm of desire as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive ignorance as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or even the state of a pratyekabuddha as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the state of a bodhisattva as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata as a basis for apprehension. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. [234,ii] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, by what means does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through skillful means. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, what is this skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift while dedicating it to all sentient beings. He guards morality while dedicating it to all sentient beings. He cultivates patience while dedicating it to all sentient beings. He exerts vigor while dedicating it to all sentient beings. He dwells in meditative concentration while dedicating it to all sentient beings. He cultivates wisdom while dedicating it to all sentient beings. He dedicates all roots of goodness—whether they arise from giving, guarding morality, cultivating patience, exerting vigor, dwelling in meditative concentration, or cultivating wisdom—to the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings. This, Subhūti, is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
