This is not correct. Now, my friend, you must explain this: is eligibility (*adhikāra*) dependent upon one’s capacity (*śakti*), such that the performance (*prayoga*) is according to that eligibility; or is eligibility dependent upon the scriptural injunction (*śruti*), while the performance by one who is eligible is according to his capacity? In the former case, just as in a rite associated with a specific time, only those living at that time are eligible because others lack the capability to perform that specific rite, so too would there be a transgression of eligibility for one who does not perform it even at other times. In the latter case, however, since the capacity for the subsidiaries (*aṅga-śakti*) would not qualify the eligibility, it would follow that the rite must be performed continuously. We do not say that the capacity for the subsidiaries qualifies the eligibility; rather, we say that eligibility itself depends upon the capacity for the subsidiaries. Thus, if a particular subsidiary is impossible for someone, the performance simply does not take place. Furthermore, it has been stated that due to deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), the very cause of eligibility for the fruit does not exist.

[236,i] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the eye as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive forms as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the earth element as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive ignorance as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive generosity as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, or Arhatship as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive the state of a Buddha as a basis for apprehension. Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as a basis for apprehension. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-apprehensible, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving? How can he train in the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom? How can he train in the fruit of a Stream-enterer? How can he train in the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, or Arhatship? How can he train in the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha? How can he train in the state of a Buddha? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he gives a gift without perceiving a giver, without perceiving a recipient, and without perceiving a gift. This is called the perfection of giving of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he observes morality without perceiving morality, without perceiving a transgression, and without perceiving one who observes morality. This is called the perfection of morality of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he is patient toward all beings without perceiving a self, without perceiving others, and without perceiving patience. This is called the perfection of patience of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he exerts vigor without perceiving vigor, without perceiving laziness, and without perceiving one who exerts vigor. This is called the perfection of vigor of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he enters into meditative absorption without perceiving concentration, without perceiving distraction, and without perceiving one who enters into meditative absorption. This is called the perfection of meditation of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he develops wisdom without perceiving wisdom, without perceiving ignorance, and without perceiving one who develops wisdom. This is called the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he trains in the fruit of a Stream-enterer without apprehending it; he trains in the fruit of a Once-returner without apprehending it; he trains in the fruit of a Non-returner without apprehending it; he trains in Arhatship without apprehending it; he trains in the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha without apprehending it; and he trains in the state of a Buddha without apprehending it. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generate the thought of enlightenment? How can he practice the six perfections? How can he enter the stages? How can he purify the buddha-fields? How can he mature sentient beings? How can he turn the wheel of Dharma? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are empty, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generates the thought of enlightenment through the power of great compassion. Because of great compassion, he practices the six perfections. Because of the six perfections, he enters the stages. Because of entering the stages, he purifies the buddha-fields. Because of purifying the buddha-fields, he matures sentient beings. Because of maturing sentient beings, he turns the wheel of Dharma. Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are empty, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not abandon the work of a Buddha because of his great compassion."

What is this "impossibility"? It is the incapacity to perform the ritual in its entirety. If that were the case, then such a person would not be eligible [for the rite], because that [incapacity] serves as a qualification for it. Alternatively, if there is no performance of the rite, it is simply a non-constituent factor. Occasional incapacity is what constitutes "impossibility"; one is not excluded from eligibility on that account, just as one is not excluded from eligibility due to a deficiency in a constituent part that cannot be remedied by the substance [of the sacrifice]. True; however, unlike a Śūdra, [eligibility does not cease] absolutely. Rather, when the cause of eligibility is absent, the eligibility itself does not cease, just as the eligibility of one who desires a fruit does not cease when the desire for the fruit has vanished. Otherwise, if eligibility were lost upon the occasional failure of the capacity for a constituent part—even though the result is not produced—the one who was eligible, capable, and desiring heaven, would have overstepped his eligibility while performing [the rite] at an improper time.

[239,i] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this is the first great miracle of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he can cause all the waters of the great ocean—four million, three hundred thousand, and thirty-six thousand yojanas in depth—to remain suspended in mid-air, like a single drop of water on a lotus leaf, for as long as he desires. This, Ānanda, is the second great miracle of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he can cause all the great earth, extending for thousands of yojanas, to be covered by a single step, and to rise up again from that very spot. This, Ānanda, is the third great miracle of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he can cause all the great earth to be covered by a single step, and to rise up again from that very spot. This, Ānanda, is the fourth great miracle of the Tathāgata. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Blessed One! How vast is the power of the Tathāgata’s supernormal knowledge and vision! How great is the majesty of the Tathāgata’s supernormal knowledge and vision! The Blessed One said: “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. It is wonderful, Ānanda, how vast is the power of the Tathāgata’s supernormal knowledge and vision, and how great is the majesty of the Tathāgata’s supernormal knowledge and vision. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has fully realized the unconditioned, the uncreated, the unarisen, the unproduced, and the non-manifested. Since he has fully realized these, he knows them as they truly are. And because he knows them as they truly are, he possesses the supernormal knowledge and vision of a Tathāgata. It is through this supernormal knowledge and vision that the Tathāgata performs such great miracles. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the name of this discourse on the Dharma? The Blessed One said: “Therefore, Ānanda, you should remember this discourse on the Dharma as ‘The Great Miracles,’ and also as ‘The Exposition of the Supernormal Knowledges. [239,i]

Now, even one who is entitled [to perform a rite] does not overstep his entitlement by failing to perform it during the period of impurity (kāla-śauca) when he has a son born, because the immediate sequence of the occasion (*nimitta-anantarya*) is not what is expressed by the words of the injunction. Even if the time is met, one who performs the rite while awaiting the completion of other auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) would be acting in the same way. If, on the other hand, it is argued that life itself as delimited by the time that constitutes an auxiliary factor is the cause of entitlement, then the same applies to other auxiliaries. Furthermore, why would one who is entitled with all parts complete perform the rite with deficient parts? If you say "because it is impossible," we say no, for that is overwhelmed by three possible hypotheses. To explain: either the non-performance is due to the fact that the mandate (*niyoga*) depends on the completion of the action and thus the entitlement is not fulfilled; or it is due to the force of the entitlement itself; or it is due to compliance with the instruction of the additional parts as far as possible. When such a person is capable, then—since both [the mandate and the parts] are favored and since immediate sequence is not what is expressed by the words—it is proper to say "when" (*yadā*), just as in the case of the *Jātaputreṣṭi*. Or, the non-performance is due to the lack of capacity in the auxiliary parts, just as in the case of time. Nor can a single injunction be both the motivator and the non-motivator of those very parts. Moreover, for what purpose does one engage in a rite with deficient parts? We reply: "For the fulfillment of the entitlement. Is the fulfillment of the entitlement independent of the parts, like the fulfillment of the fruit? If so, then they are simply not parts at all. If it is dependent, then it must be accomplished by the parts according to one's capacity; thus, in the case of deficiency, the effort would be in vain. If you say it is accomplished by the parts according to capacity, this is not sufficient to establish a distinction in the nature of the task. Furthermore, the fruit arises from the entitlement; in that case, for one entitled to perform the rite endowed with parts according to capacity, the fulfillment of the entitlement occurs through that very [performance], as if caused by it. If it is not so, then there would be no fulfillment of the entitlement. For one entitled to perform the rite with all parts complete, performing it with deficient parts is like performing a different ritual act altogether; here, the distinction between auxiliary and principal is irrelevant, because there is no difference insofar as they are objects of the injunction of entitlement. And if there were a difference, it would follow that the auxiliary is not a part at all. Moreover, the relationship of auxiliary and principal cannot be determined [in this context].
It has been stated that even if there were an injunction, since the purpose would not be accomplished, it would follow that the effort is in vain.

And what is this "qualification" (*adhikāra*) whose fulfillment (*nirvṛtti*) is at issue? If it is "being enjoined" (*niyoga*), then there is no fulfillment, because one who is enjoined has not yet acted. If it is "being subject to an injunction" (*niyojyatā*), that too is fulfilled only through the injunction itself. If it is "ownership" (*svāmitā*), then one who does not enjoy anything produced by that [injunction] is not an owner; thus, both types of qualification would be dependent on the completion of the action. Therefore, the distinction between the qualifications for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites cannot be established on the grounds of whether they terminate in the action or in the application (*prayoga*); it must be explained otherwise.
That is explained as follows:
Since the causes, such as livelihood and the like, are equal, time is the distinguishing factor;
when the rite has been performed for the sake of that cause, there is a necessity to perform it again.

First, one who is entirely incapable of the aforementioned performance is excluded from the entitlement (*adhikāra*) altogether; such a person cannot be understood as being subject to the injunction. Therefore, the understanding of entitlement belongs only to one who is capable, depending upon both the capacity (*śakti*) and the instruction of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Furthermore, this understanding of entitlement does not result in a permanent obligation because capacity is non-eternal. Otherwise, if there were no performance of all the auxiliaries by one who is entitled, there would be no performance at all; or else, if performance were according to what is possible, then since the entitlement would belong to one of a different sort, a performance of that kind would not be scriptural (*aśāstrīya*), and thus there would be no performance due to a lack of entitlement. Consequently, capacity is required once again for the final determination of the understanding of entitlement. For it has been stated that capacity is a single part of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); it is not for the sake of determining the performance itself, because that [performance] has no other means of knowledge. That [capacity] may be resorted to either in terms of time or in terms of the auxiliaries. In that regard, if one resorts to it in terms of the auxiliaries, there is a contradiction with the scripture because of the abandonment of other auxiliaries understood from the words. But in terms of time, since other times are not the meaning of the words, there is no contradiction whatsoever. And this absence of contradiction exists when the entitlement is without a condition (*animitta*), because the meaning of the word consists merely in "this [act] is to be done by this [person] in this way. However, when there is a condition (*sanimitta*), there is a contradiction with the hearing of the condition, because once that [condition] has arrived, the fact that the act is caused by that [condition] is subverted. If it is argued that in the other case (the obligatory) there is also a contradiction with the hearing of "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), it has already been stated: the specification of a particular person is not intended here, because it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Nor is there continuous performance, because the duty is understood as having a specific time when there is a condition, since the time specifically qualifies it by implication (*arthāt*), as it enters into the condition itself. As it has been said: "Time is not an auxiliary (*guṇa*), for this is a condition"; the meaning is that it is not merely an auxiliary. But other auxiliaries are not like this, because of the inequality and the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). For other auxiliaries are things to be taken up (*upādeya*), whereas the condition is not to be taken up. The mode of expression regarding the auxiliaries is "one should do these by means of these," while regarding the condition it is "when this exists. Therefore, other auxiliaries are not able to enter into the condition. But time, being not to be taken up, shares the same mode of expression and, even while being an auxiliary, properly enters into the condition. Now, why is the inclusion of the condition alone not desired? Even in the case of a desire-based rite (*kāmya*), it occurs by the desire for that time. Is this not the purpose? True. But the reason is that the hearing of "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva*) has no meaning beyond this, and also that the principal rite (*prakaraṇin*) serves the purpose of the auxiliaries. Thus, because there is no contradiction, in the case of a conditionless rite, the resort to capacity is in terms of time—i.e., "when [the time] occurs"—but in the case of one possessing a condition, because of the contradiction with the condition, it is "as it is" in terms of the auxiliaries, provided they possess the time.

But what is this that is contradicted? It is the locus of power in terms of time. And from what is it understood whose [power] it is? How is the relationship between cause and effect established? And how does this [power] have a causal connection? If it means "when this exists," what is the contradiction? For even in terms of time, when that locus of power does not exist, its activity does not exist; yet when it does exist, the activity occurs. There would indeed be a contradiction if it meant "only when this exists. But such is not the meaning of "cause" (*nimitta*). For a cause is a *nimitta*. And causes do not necessarily possess their effects. However, an effect does not exist when the cause is absent. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

If the cause [of the injunction] is the ritual action (*karman*), then the injunction is rendered useless because the performance of the action proceeds from that very cause. Furthermore, since one observes those possessing a cause even when the cause is not specifically determined, there would be an absence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*). Its production does not arise from that cause, because it is eternal. When that [cause] exists, there is no cognition [of the result], because that is established by the sentence alone; thus, the ritual action is useless. If it is argued that "it occurs only when [the cause] exists," meaning that the fruit of the ritual action arises only when that [cause] is present, then there is no contradiction regarding the inclusion of all constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*). Alternatively, if it is argued that the qualification (*adhikāra*) [is the cause], we say no; for qualification arises from the mandate (*niyoga*). That very connection with the mandate is what is caused by that [qualification]. If, then, the mandate has that as its cause, the understanding of the cause does not come from the mandate itself. Since that [mandate] is expressed by the word as depending on a cause already established, there is a state of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*).

[255,i] Now, the status of the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) as a causal condition (*nimitta*) follows by implication, because there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) when that condition exists. Neither perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge apply here, nor does verbal testimony (*śabda*), because the latter has injunction (*vidhi*) as its primary object, and that [injunction] has only positive entities (*bhāva*) as its domain, and because it exceeds the three factors (*aṃśatraya*) of an action. In that case, since the action being enjoined is enjoined with respect to the fruit, if both [the fruit and the condition] were enjoined in that injunction, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

It is said: That in whose presence there is a necessity to perform an action is the cause for that [action]. How so? When something exists and [the effect] necessarily follows, that is the primary cause; the other, however, is [a cause] figuratively, due to its connection with a particular state. And between the secondary and the primary, the understanding applies to the primary; thus, the necessity is established by the very power of being the cause for that [action]. For that would not even be a cause if, when it exists, the action were not performed.

Furthermore, the necessity of performing an action (*avaśyakarttavyatā*) as it is understood does not apply to an action whose entirety of constituent parts (*aṅga*) must be gathered together, nor to that which is never a means to what is beneficial; therefore, it is understood that the action is always a desired means when it is endowed with its constituent parts according to one's capacity. Moreover, the status of being a "condition" (*nimittatā*) belongs to the necessity of performance, which takes the form of an injunction (*vidhi*). When that condition exists, for one who performs it in whatever manner possible, it certainly accomplishes the destruction of sin, which is always the desired goal. Even though it is an absence (*bhāvavyatireka*), it is an object of knowledge through verbal testimony (*śabdaprameyatva*); for although it is not itself something to be enjoined, it enters into the injunction just like an enjoined thing, because it is a qualification of the injunction. For this very reason, there is no room for an option (*vikalpa*) regarding its connection with the ritual action; thus, the argument is sound.

[258,i] But is it not the case that they consider qualifiers of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), such as "living" and so forth, to be like "heaven" and so forth, because the person to be enjoined is required first by the injunction? For no injunction is seen in the world that does not depend on a specific qualifier of the person to be enjoined; in its absence, there would be no comprehension at all. However, that very qualifier, when present, stands as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the injunction, whereas heaven and the like stand as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by virtue of being desired.

This is not sound, because the qualification is untenable. For there is no one who is ever qualified by "as long as life" (*yāvaj-jīvam*) or by "various spring seasons" (*aneka-vasanta-kāla-viśiṣṭaḥ*) such that he could be enjoined [to perform the rite]. Neither mere living nor mere springtime constitutes a qualification, because living is not something to be expressed [as a condition], and because the terms "as long as" (*yāvat*) and "repetition" (*vīpsā*) would lack syntactic connection. Nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) of two things already established; for even for one who lives and desires heaven, there is no contradiction in the entitlement (*adhikāra*) due to the restrictive adjunct (*upabandha*) "when he is able. Since the injunction requires everything up to the sequence [of performance], there is no loss of its subsidiary elements (*aṅga*). Therefore, because the meanings of "as long as" and "repetition" do not connect, living is not a qualification of the agent, as it is not something to be expressed; likewise, the phrase "in every spring" is not a connection with a temporal meaning. Thus, that is merely a contingent cause (*nimitta*). For instance:

[261,i] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā-svabhāva*). These, Mahāmati, are called the four kinds of self-nature. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the self-nature of discrimination is that which is grasped by the ignorant and simple-minded through the habit-energy of false discrimination; it is like seeing a rope and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the self-nature of discrimination. The self-nature of dependent origination, Mahāmati, refers to the manifestation of various phenomena based on the causal conditions of the habit-energy of false discrimination. It is like a mirage in the springtime, where various forms appear due to the power of past karma. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. The self-nature of perfect accomplishment, Mahāmati, is the realization that the self-nature of dependent origination is devoid of the characteristics of the self-nature of discrimination. It is like seeing the rope for what it truly is once the delusion of the snake has ceased. This is called the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. The self-nature of the ultimate reality, Mahāmati, is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, which is eternally free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, and is realized by noble wisdom. This is called the self-nature of the ultimate reality. These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of self-nature. By means of these four kinds of self-nature, Mahāmati, one enters into the Tathāgata-garbha, which is the realm of the noble ones. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself in this way.

There is no non-connection between these two; for that [condition] would not even be a *nimitta* (occasioning cause) if the rite were not performed when it exists. Furthermore, since the qualification of the person entitled to perform the act (*adhikāriviśeṣa*) is established by the rule that "the injunction belongs to one who possesses the occasion," there is no lack of comprehension. Therefore, the occasion is a qualifier of the person entitled to the act while existing as an occasion, but it is not an occasion while being a qualifier of the person entitled to the act. Moreover, because the status of being an occasion is based on the word itself, the following is improper: to abandon the direct meaning of the word and, by the power of the word, treat it as primarily intended for that [occasion], while treating the other meaning as secondary by implication. For the suffixes such as the optative (*liṅg*) express this through various Smṛti rules, such as "one should burn [the body] when [it is] broken" or "one beginning [the rite]. Just as an occasion is a qualifier of the person entitled to the act while being an occasion, so too a fruit is a qualifier of the person entitled to the act while being a fruit; it is not a fruit while being a qualifier of the person entitled to the act—this has been stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka*.

[263,i] Although that [inquiry] was previously required, it belongs strictly to the stage of comprehension (*pratipatti*), because comprehension depends upon performance (*anuṣṭhāna*); thus, the final determination occurs at the very end of the sequence.

[263,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from their suffering. Then, at that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, with single-minded devotion, call upon him, he will immediately provide them with protection and deliverance, freeing them from all suffering. Ānanda, if there be a great multitude of people traveling on a perilous sea, and they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, they shall immediately be delivered from the perils of the sea. Ānanda, if there be robbers who intend to plunder a village, and they encounter a person who invokes the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, they shall immediately abandon their evil intent and depart. Ānanda, if there be a woman who desires a son or a daughter, and she invokes the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, she shall immediately give birth to a son or daughter who possesses auspicious marks, is endowed with wisdom and virtue, and is beloved by all. Thus spoke the Bhagavān. Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One further addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, if there be sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to worship the relics of the Tathāgata, they should fashion images of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, whether made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, emerald, or other precious substances; or fashioned from clay, wood, lacquer, or cloth; or painted in colors; or carved from stone, metal, or ivory; or even fashioned from cow dung or mud. Whether they place them in stūpas or in temples, or simply keep them in their homes, they should always offer flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, banners, and canopies. By doing so, they shall obtain immeasurable merit and be able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions. Ānanda, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower. Therefore, you should all respectfully revere and honor him. At that time, the entire assembly, having heard what the Bhagavān had said, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. Thus ends the Chapter on the Universal Gateway of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in the Lotus Sutra. The twenty-fifth chapter, titled “The Universal Gateway of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. [264,i] Chapter Twenty-Six: The Former Deeds of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāparibhūta. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha: “Bhagavān, I have now seen the great spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, and I have heard the Dharma preached by the Buddha. Bhagavān, if there be sons of good family or daughters of good family who hear this Lotus Sutra and, having heard it, believe and accept it, how much more so if they read, recite, copy, and explain it to others! Bhagavān, such persons shall be known to have performed the deeds of a Buddha. Why is this? Because, Bhagavān, this Lotus Sutra is the king of all sutras, supreme and unsurpassed. It is the treasury of the Tathāgatas, the secret Dharma of the Buddhas, and the most profound and subtle teaching. Bhagavān, if there be those who hear this sutra and do not slander it, they shall be known to have planted roots of goodness under many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas. Bhagavān, if there be those who, having heard this sutra, believe and accept it, they shall be known to have attained the stage of non-retrogression. Why is this? Because, Bhagavān, this Lotus Sutra is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is, Śāriputra. As you say, this Lotus Sutra is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas. Surely, if this were the case, then because the desired result (*iṣṭa*) is attached to every instance involving an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be an absence of an original injunction (*utpatti-codanā*). Consequently, due to their mutual independence, even when they are in proximity, there would be no repetition of the scriptural statement for the sake of the result; thus, there would be a distinction of rites (*karma-bheda*) everywhere, and it could not be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Furthermore, in the case of "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), there would be no connection between the accessory (*guṇa*) and the result. Nor is anything else desired [as a result] other than happiness (*sukha*), and since that is heaven (*svarga*), the scope for cattle and the like would be difficult to find because heaven would already be occupied. Or, if they were included by way of being taken up (*upādāna*), then heaven would become permanent (*nitya*). Therefore, what remains as the object of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)? Its very status as a human goal (*puruṣārthatā*) is the qualification. Even so, when there is a condition (*nimitta*), the rite itself must be the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*); otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) regarding the condition and the result, both of which would be things to be adopted (*upādeya*), resulting in the incongruity of "by living one performs the oblation" and "by the oblation one obtains the result. This is because two things to be aimed at cannot coexist in a single sentence. Indeed, it is not easy to derive both the destruction of evil and the avoidance of misfortune from a single act, especially when there is no action involved. And thus, because the form of the rite is already known, it cannot be a subordinate member (*anaṅga*), and therefore there is no adoption [of the rite] according to one's capacity.
It is said:
[The nature of injunction consists of] origination, application, purpose, performance, and qualification.
The entire ritual procedure is not differentiated because of the specific quality of being directed toward that [single goal].

An injunction (*vidhi*) does not consist merely in the fact that something is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), but rather in the agent’s *evam-kāram* (the state of "doing thus"). Furthermore, the cognition of "instigation" (*pravartanā*) is the indicator [of the injunction], because otherwise there would be an absence of a cause for activity. For even if something is a means to what is desired, one does not act toward it if it is already established by itself or by another source, and its operation is thus not required. As it has been said: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its defining characteristic. This is because the scripture is characterized by being a means to the fruit of the performer. Consequently, from the scripture—which is synonymous with an injunction—the performance of the action is understood. Moreover, regarding an action whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), its specific nature is also dependent upon the scripture, since it was not previously established prior to the injunction. And when [the action] is required, there is "application" (*viniyoga*) because it is a means to what is required. Furthermore, there must be some qualified person (*adhikārī*) or master who is to be instigated, for whom this is a means to his desired end. In all cases, although these four factors are perceived, their primary intent (*aidamparya*) differs. Therefore, there is a distinction between the types of injunctions, such as those of origin (*utpatti-vidhi*) and so forth. That primary intent arises from the connection with a specific word expressing attainment (*prāpti*) or a particular supplement (*upapada*). Sometimes there is intent toward all four, as in "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*"; because nothing else [for origin, application, etc. is obtained from elsewhere, and because of the connection with a word denoting the fruit. Sometimes there is intent toward three, as in the sentence concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, because the origin is obtained from elsewhere. Sometimes there is intent toward two, as in the sentence concerning the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, because both origin and connection are established from elsewhere. Sometimes there is intent toward only one, as in "He performs the *agnihotra*" or "One should sacrifice on the full moon day. In these cases, there is no application (*viniyoga*) to a fruit, because it is impossible to cognize a specific fruit that has not been specified. If that is not specified, there is no cognition of a specific qualified person (*adhikārī*), and thus no qualification (*adhikāra*). For this very reason, there is no performance (*prayoga*). Indeed, the cognition of performance does not become stable unless the status of being a means to a desired end is established, nor can it be established without a determined performer. Therefore, the cognition of performance arises precisely from the sentence stating the fruit. Thus, in the case of "He performs the *agnihotra*," the injunction is intent upon the essential nature of the ritual act (*karman*). The other parts, though cognized, are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). However, in the case of "On the full moon day," because it is not intent upon anything else, there is intent toward the distinction of performance. In the case of acts like sprinkling (*saṃmārga*) or purifying (*prokṣaṇa*), however, the intent is toward origin and application; for once the instrumental part of the primary sacrifice is attained through the medium of rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth, the performance is accomplished by the injunction of the instrument itself, and because the qualified person has the cognition of qualification (*adhikāra*). Some maintain that in the case of the *samidh* offerings and others, there is intent toward origin alone, because application is based on a verbal text (*śruti*) inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*). But here, it is the verbal text itself—inferred from the context—that is the applicator (*viniyojikā*). This very injunction is the basis for application. Now, if the applicators are the verbal text and so forth (*śrutyādayaḥ*), what is the need for an injunction here? This is not so. For application is the state of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*), and that belongs to the injunction. The verbal text and so forth, however, are causes for mere relationship. And relationship is of many kinds, such as the relation of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). But the state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) belongs to the injunction. How then are the verbal text and so forth applicators? Because when something is understood to be related to another by means of the verbal text and so forth, while its being for the sake of another is being presented by the injunction, the cognition arises: "This is for the sake of that. Nor has the definition of the subordinate (*śeṣa*) been stated as having both characteristics; for that is the domain of the injunction. And that intent toward the essential nature [of the act] has been considered in the section on "Distinction" (*Bhedalakṣaṇa*), because distinction depends upon it. For an injunction intent upon the essential nature differentiates the ritual act.

Furthermore, even when a single word is employed, because there is a fixed rule of precedence between the root and the suffix within the nature of *bhāvanā*, the expression of the meaning by the suffix—dependent upon the meaning of the root—is perceived only when it has been linked to its grammatical connection (*anubandha*). Since a pure [suffix] is not obtained [independently], its capacity to be intent upon enjoining the meaning of the verbal root is untenable. Consequently, since it is untenable for a single *bhāvanā* to be intent upon enjoining multiple meanings of verbal roots, and because there would be no enjoiner of multiple root-meanings within a single *bhāvanā*, the entire Veda would constitute a single sentence and a single *apūrva*. However, this is not the case with the *samit* and other such [subsidiary rites], because they are not intent upon anything else.

Regarding the phrase "three oblations," although it refers to their essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is a distinction based on number. If it were not so, then that [number] would be irrelevant; but this is not the case, because even in its absence, the attainment of the number can still be achieved through repetition.
Even a subordinate element (guṇa), by precluding mere application from its prior connection, brings about precisely that state of being the primary purpose.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) as well, by cutting off previous cognition and merely through the contradiction involved in the application of qualities such as "being worthy of a thousand sacrificial gifts," produces a new cognition and brings about that very same thing.
Even another section of the treatise functions solely as a synonym for the exclusion of other cognitions.

[281,i] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. It should be preserved by you as such. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the name of this chapter of the *Sūtra of the Great Vehicle*, and how should it be remembered? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this chapter of the *Sūtra of the Great Vehicle* is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle,’ and it should be remembered by you as such. Then the venerable Ānanda, having heard the words of the Blessed One, rejoiced and put them into practice. This concludes the *Sūtra of the Great Vehicle*, the Chapter on the Exposition of the Great Vehicle, the twenty-eighth. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "If there is a bhikṣu who, having committed an offense, does not confess it, he commits two transgressions: first, the transgression of the offense itself; second, the transgression of not confessing it. If he later confesses it, he is freed from the first transgression but remains subject to the second. If he does not confess it, he commits three transgressions: first, the transgression of the offense itself; second, the transgression of not confessing it; third, the transgression of concealing it. If he later confesses it, he is freed from the first two transgressions but remains subject to the third. If he does not confess it, he commits four transgressions: first, the transgression of the offense itself; second, the transgression of not confessing it; third, the transgression of concealing it; fourth, the transgression of increasing the offense. If he later confesses it, he is freed from the first three transgressions but remains subject to the fourth. If he does not confess it, he commits five transgressions: first, the transgression of the offense itself; second, the transgression of not confessing it; third, the transgression of concealing it; fourth, the transgression of increasing the offense; fifth, the transgression of further increasing the offense. If he later confesses it, he is freed from the first four transgressions but remains subject to the fifth. If he does not confess it, he commits six transgressions: first, the transgression of the offense itself; second, the transgression of not confessing it; third, the transgression of concealing it; fourth, the transgression of increasing the offense; fifth, the transgression of further increasing the offense; sixth, the transgression of further increasing the offense again. But because that [connection] is not interrupted in the case of *sannidhi* (proximity), there is no [need for] *tātparya* (intentional focus); thus, it is "non-interruption. And so, the fact that ritual action (*karman*) is to be enjoined is an introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*) regarding its various types. However, the focus on *viniyoga* (application) will be explained in the third book (*adhyāya*). For it has been stated that the purposefulness [of a thing] does not arise from *śruti* (direct statement) and the other means alone; nor is that [purposefulness] established without recourse to performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). And performance belongs to the injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, that too is intended to be expressed. True. But since that is established through the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), this [present section] is concerned solely with *viniyoga*. As it has been said: "In this way, the injunction of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*); yet, nothing becomes a subsidiary unless it is enjoined, therefore, for the sake of being a subsidiary, it must be enjoined."

In this regard, since application (*viniyoga*) is based on direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, and since an injunction (*vidhi*) consists merely in impelling, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) belongs only to substances and the like, and thus the injunction is not an applicator. To this it is replied: even the form of impelling would be difficult to obtain if there were no applicatory power; therefore, the capacity for application has been stated according to the method to be explained in the sūtra, "But it is not an accomplisher because it exists for the sake of that" (*asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt*).

If it is suspected that the injunction (*vidhi*) alone is the applicator (*viniyojaka*) and that the direct statement (*śruti*) and other means are not causes, it is stated later on that [the injunction] is dependent upon the direct statement and the rest.
In the fourth chapter, however, there is an investigation into the number of subsidiaries as they constitute the factors for performance.

How so? That which depends on the performance of the injunctions for a sacrifice (*kratu*) is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); that which proceeds based on the desire of a person (*puruṣa*) is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). In this regard, there arises an inquiry into what is prompted (*prayojaka*) and what is not prompted (*aprayojaka*), considering: "What is performed by virtue of an injunction for a sacrifice? To what extent does the operation of the sacrificial injunction extend? Or, in what case is it for the person, due to other causes independent of that injunction? By means of such an inquiry, the scope of the operation of the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice is determined.

To explain: the injunction for the performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice, being for the purpose of the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), enforces the bringing of the curds (*dadhyānayana*), but not for the sake of the *vājina* (whey), because only that which is produced as a byproduct of that [primary purpose] can enter into it. Likewise, this applies to the seventh footprint (*pada*) which is brought about as an inseparable concomitant of the act of purchasing [Soma]. Similarly, the potsherd (*kapāla*) belongs only to the remnant of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); since it comes into contact with it through the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*), and since the northern half [of the cake] is merely a part [of the whole], the part already taken up cannot be a further object of acquisition—thus, there is no separate performance [of the action for the potsherd].

For if [the passage] were an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), then the performance of qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood would be based on the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice (*kratu-prayoga-vidhi*) which has the *juhū* ladle and other components as its object; whereas in the case of an injunction of a result (*phala-vidhi*), that basis would be absent. Therefore, an *arthavāda* serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), while an injunction of a result serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, even though the performance of being made of *parṇa*-wood is dependent on an injunction, it serves the purpose of the person because it is not the object of the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice. The scope of that operation has been considered in this very way. As for the primary act (*pradhāna*), although the engagement [of the agent] arises from the injunction in a specific form, it exists in a general form with respect to the person; it is by virtue of this much that it serves the purpose of the person. However, the requirement for subsidiaries (*aṅga*) follows after the knowledge of the instrument (*karaṇa*); since the knowledge of that [instrument] is the injunction for it, and because engagement even in a general sense depends upon it, the subsidiary serves the purpose of the sacrifice. But then, how is it that "one [act] is a motivator (*prayojaka*) serving the purpose of the person, while another is non-motivating (*aprayojaka*) serving the purpose of the sacrifice"? What is the point here? For here, the two things to be motivated—those serving the purpose of the sacrifice and those serving the purpose of the person—have been mentioned. In that case, it should have been stated: "one thing to be motivated serves the purpose of the person, and another serves the purpose of the sacrifice. This is not a fault. The terms "serving the purpose of the person" (*puruṣārtha*) and "serving the purpose of the sacrifice" (*kratvartha*) form a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*), because the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which is for the purpose of the person" (*puruṣasyārthaḥ*).

This is what is meant: for someone, something is an object to be employed; this is the sense. Even in the case of an injunction regarding a sacrifice (*kratu-vidhi*), there is something to be employed and something not to be employed, as in the case of the bringing of curd (*dadhyānayana*) by way of the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina*. In that context, it has been shown that performance occurs in the portion consisting of the fruit—according to the principle "in that which there is pleasure"—and not by virtue of an injunction. Furthermore, the fact that the fruit of the *śyena*-sacrifice and others is harmful (*anarthatva*) is established by the definition of the "subordinate" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), based on whether they are objects of the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice or not, by virtue of being members of the sacrifice or members of those [subsidiaries]. The distinction between what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is made through an investigation into whether something is a subordinate part of the sacrifice or not. But the latter [distinction] is already established once the unity of the subordinate parts is proven, because it merely involves an investigation into the extent of the operation of the injunction for the sacrifice and the injunction for its performance. For this very reason it was said: "The subject matter of the third [book] has been transcended."

[293,i] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the southern region, beheld five hundred merchantmen who were about to set out upon the great ocean. He saw that they had not yet made offerings to the Three Jewels nor performed acts of charity and merit; furthermore, they were without a protective deity and lacked the power of mantras and spells. Seeing them thus, he felt great compassion for them and resolved to protect them. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara transformed himself into a merchant leader and went before the merchants. He addressed them, saying: "O merchants, you are setting out upon the great ocean; you have not yet made offerings to the Three Jewels, nor have you performed acts of charity and merit. Moreover, you lack a protective deity and are without the power of mantras and spells. You must now offer worship to the Three Jewels and perform acts of charity and merit. Furthermore, you must invoke the Great Compassionate One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, as your protector. Having spoken thus, he taught them the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: Tadyathā: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. "If you recite this mantra, you will surely be protected by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and reach the great ocean in safety. The merchants, having heard these words, all rejoiced and followed his instructions. They made offerings to the Three Jewels, performed acts of charity and merit, and invoked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara as their protector. Then, they set out upon the great ocean. At that time, a great storm arose, and a fierce wind blew from the four quarters, threatening to overturn their ship. The merchants were terrified and cried out in distress. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, hearing their cries, immediately extended his right hand across the great ocean and touched the ship. By the power of his spiritual authority, the ship was immediately turned back. The merchants, seeing this, were filled with joy and praised him, saying: "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is truly a great compassionate one; he has saved us from this perilous place. Having said this, they returned safely to their own country. This is called the second chapter on the protection of the merchants. [293,ii] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the southern region, saw five hundred bandits who were about to plunder a village. He saw that they were without a protective deity and lacked the power of mantras and spells. Seeing them thus, he felt great compassion for them and resolved to transform them. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara transformed himself into a merchant leader and went before the bandits. He addressed them, saying: "O bandits, you are about to commit evil deeds; you will surely fall into hell. You must now repent and reform, and invoke the Great Compassionate One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, as your protector. Having spoken thus, he taught them the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: Tadyathā: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. "If you recite this mantra, you will surely be protected by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and attain peace and happiness. The bandits, having heard these words, all rejoiced and followed his instructions. They repented and reformed, and invoked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara as their protector. By the power of his spiritual authority, they were all transformed into virtuous people. This is called the third chapter on the transformation of the bandits. [293,v] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the southern region, saw five hundred ghosts who were suffering from various diseases and torments. He saw that they were without a protective deity and lacked the power of mantras and spells. Seeing them thus, he felt great compassion for them and resolved to transform them. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara transformed himself into a physician and went before the ghosts. He addressed them, saying: "O ghosts, you are suffering from various diseases and torments; you will surely fall into the realm of hungry ghosts. You must now repent and reform, and invoke the Great Compassionate One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, as your protector. Having spoken thus, he taught them the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: Tadyathā: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. "If you recite this mantra, you will surely be protected by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and attain peace and happiness. But what is being considered in the fifth [book]? Is it not the question: "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the sequence [determined]? [The answer is: "By direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth. This is not sound. It has been stated that Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by an injunction (*codanā*), and that it exists in exactly four states. Sequence, however, is distinct from those; for it is not the object of the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), because it is not something to be performed. Furthermore, it is not the literal meaning of the word, because—unlike the constituent ritual acts—it cannot be defined as a specific "this" apart from them. For it is the ritual acts (*padārtha*) that are performed in a sequence, but not the sequence itself. Nor is it the object of the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) or the injunction of origin (*utpatti-vidhi*). For this very reason, it is not the object of the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), because there is no person to be enjoined (*aniyojyatva*). Granted that there might be an injunction specifically intent upon a scriptural rule of sequence, there can be no such injunction regarding meaning and the other factors. To this it is replied: It has been stated that the performance (*prayoga*) is the meaning of the injunction. And the distinction of sequence is a particularity of that performance. For it is said that the ritual acts are performed in a sequence.

And thus, because it is the object of the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), sequence (*krama*) does not transcend the characteristic of being defined by Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇatva*). In that regard, since sequence—being distinct from the first [category]—is not determined as a specific entity (*idantayā*), one might suspect it is not an object of performance, not an object of application (*aviniyojyatā*), and not something to be produced; having raised this doubt, its status as an object of the injunction of performance is demonstrated. By the subsequent section, however, the purity of the example is established, because the ritual act of initiation (*dīkṣā-padartha*) is already obtained. Even though it is not directly denoted, since the performance of a specific sequence—which is somehow cognized—is for the sake of the injunction, the connection with the *adhvaryu* priest as a specific performer would be purposeless. Furthermore, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to enjoining multiple objects. However, since the ritual act of initiation repeats for each primary rite, the injunction of a specific performance has a single purpose. In enjoining that, there is the prohibition: "One who is purified does not purify" (*na pūtaḥ pāvayati*), and "The other [is for] another," and "From which there would be a distinction among them. Because a non-Brahmin lacks the office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), and because the two later stages of life (*āśrama*) [the forest-dweller and the renunciant] do not perform it, and because the student (*brahmacārin*) is dependent on his teacher, [the sequence applies]. Now, although in the case of the [meanings of] words and so forth, the injunction refers to the ritual act itself, it nevertheless depends on the purpose of that form, and depends on the requirement for the restriction of the order of recitation as made known by the injunction of Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*). And while conforming to the already determined sequence, and not contradicting the understood state of co-existence, it establishes a specific performance; thus, it is indeed a limb of the performance (*prayoga-aṅga*). This was considered previously. True, it is the number of things to be performed (*prayojya-iyattā*). But sequence is not something to be performed; rather, it is a specific mode of performance. Therefore, since it was not established by the previous [section], this consideration of a specific performance constitutes a different purpose for the definition.

In the sixth [chapter], however, the portion concerning eligibility (*adhikāra*) is examined. This is because capacity—whether it belongs to one capable of performing all auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) or to another—is scriptural, owing to the distinction between what is scripturally enjoined and what is not. In this regard, just as being the means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is the cause for engagement and nothing else, so too is capability (*śakyatva*). Capability, entering into the form of the injunction (*vidhi*) which consists of impulsion (*pravartanā*), is understood through scripture just like being the means to a desired end. Thus, the action is the means to a desired end for anyone who desires it, and it is capable of being performed; having been understood from scripture, it is established according to possibility without contradiction by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it was stated that there is universal eligibility. [Objection: Since capability is the object of another means of knowledge, it is not something already established [by scripture]; therefore, the scripture would be purposeful [only] if it were included within the form of the injunction itself. However, the injunction is perceived by the word as depending on a capability that is accessible through other means of knowledge. Nor does this entail the fault of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), just as in the case of depending on the nature of things that fall within the scope of other means of knowledge. Otherwise, everyone would be capable of performing all auxiliary elements. If it is asked, "Why is there a restriction according to possibility? [we reply]: "Because of contradiction with other means of knowledge. [Response: Alas! In that case, the word would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*). One must accept that the subject matter of the scripture is the specific nature of a thing, established by definition or other means of knowledge, which is the means to comprehension and is not the object of anything else. And thus, for one who lacks the capability, there is no cause for engagement, because he is not an agent. It is understood that one who is incapable is not to be engaged therein; hence, there is eligibility for the capable. "A sentence has action as its primary element and possesses a single meaning. For those who maintain that it is action alone that is brought into being (*bhāvyate*), while substance and quality are established by their own nature, they consider the fruit (*phala*) to be unconnected to the sentence. And thus, due to the absence of a fruit, there is an absence of qualification (*adhikāra*). Indeed, no one is enjoined (*niyojya*) nor is anyone a master (*svāmī*) regarding actions that lack a fruit. But how is the fruit unconnected? Because action is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and two things to be accomplished cannot coexist in a single unity. To explain: if sacrifices and the like are themselves the actions, then they are understood as the primary elements through their sequential nature (as having prior and posterior parts). Even if there were an action distinct from them, and that action were transitive with the thing to be produced as its primary element, even then [the fruit would remain unconnected]. Why? Because of the rule of priority and posteriority. Since a suffix denotes its own meaning as connected to the meaning of the stem, [the action] is perceived as something to be accomplished. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between words for substances and qualities, and because [the rule] "of those which arise... is not accepted. Furthermore, because of the direct connection with the instrument, as in "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*). Now, one might object: "This would not be so because of the connection with another object (*karman*). No; for even in the case of an object, the traditional rule of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) applies, and it is only as a factor that it connects with the action. Its status as the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) is a matter for other means of knowledge. Thus, let there be fruitfulness in cases where the fruit is visible; but in sacrifices and the like, there is no fruit such as heaven, because of this lack of connection and the absence of other means of knowledge. And so it was said: "those [actions] are of two kinds. Otherwise, they would all be of one kind.

Thus, it is first of all logical that in the connection of substances with an action, the relationship is as a *guṇa* (subordinate factor), not as a result (*phala*). And in reality, there is no relationship [of the substance] as a result; for human effort has the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth as its object, whereas heaven (*svarga*) and the like have no such connection. Furthermore, since no other operation (*vyāpāra*) is observed in the sacrifice and so forth, their status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is untenable. Nor can there be an injunction regarding what is already accomplished (*bhūti*), because that is devoid of operation. Moreover, since an injunction applies to what is capable [of being performed], the command "one should produce heaven" would be untenable; it would also lead to the undesirable consequence that [the act] must necessarily be performed. This is because it is accepted that the result is not something to be enjoined, while the sacrifice and so forth are taken to be what is enjoined. Indeed, an injunction pertains to the object of activity, neither directly to the sacrifice nor to the result. And activity is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). That verbal expression which is the cause of the activity directed toward a particular object is called an injunction (*vidhi*). In that case, there is no productive urge (*bhāvanā*) introduced by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) that could be enjoined. Even if a distinct productive urge exists, there is no inherent connection (*samavāya*) between the sacrifice and the result as the object and the content of that urge. Nor does another result arise through the power of the injunction, because that too would lack such a connection. This is due to the dual nature [of the sacrifice and the result] and the difficulty in comprehending their status as means.
