Nor can it be established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because that would result in the loss of its defining characteristic as being of the nature of consciousness (*cetanā*). This is because such [an action] culminates in being something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*); for in the world, an action that lacks a fruit is never seen to be something to be accomplished. Furthermore, since the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is preceded by the status of being an end (*sādhyatva*), it is impossible for the latter to imply the former by way of presumption (*arthāt*). Moreover, that which is currently in the state of being an end (*purobhāvinaḥ sādhyatvasya*) lacks the capacity to imply the status of being a means. Even if there were such an implication, the agent’s form would not be "one-eyed" (i.e., incomplete) for the sake of establishing [the action]. How, then, is there an injunction (*vidhi*) now? What is the point here of asking "how"? An injunction is merely the act of impelling (*pravarttanāmātra*); it does not touch upon the human goals of benefit or harm. Why? Because it is so understood and because there is no deviation from this fact. Thus, from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, there is the comprehension of an instigation (*preraṇā*). And although being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is the cause of activity, the word, however, does not grasp that specific form; rather, it settles upon the mere cause of activity. This is because such a form is understood in cases like commands (*praiṣa*) and the like, whereas that [specific form of being a means] is absent there. Furthermore, the mere act of impelling is invariable [in all cases], whereas the fault of having multiple meanings would otherwise arise. Nor is the understanding of that [impulsion] derived solely from the understanding of that specific form [of being a means], because delusion (*moha*) and other factors are also possible.

[313,i] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of reverential salutation; they are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? They are: the Stream-enterer, the Once-returner, the Non-returner, and the Arhat. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One would teach the Dharma concerning the four fruits of the ascetic life, so that those who have not yet heard it may hear it, and those who have already heard it may gain further clarity. The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, listen attentively and bear it well in mind; I shall speak. “Even so, Blessed One,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke: “Ānanda, what are the four fruits of the ascetic life? They are: the fruit of Stream-entry, the fruit of Once-returning, the fruit of Non-returning, and the fruit of Arhatship. And what, Ānanda, is the fruit of Stream-entry? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an Arhat, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unexcelled leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He also possesses unwavering confidence in the Dharma: ‘The Dharma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. He also possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, he has abandoned the five lower fetters. This, Ānanda, is called the fruit of Stream-entry. And what, Ānanda, is the fruit of Once-returning? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... unwavering confidence in the Dharma... unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha... Furthermore, he has attenuated the three fetters—sensual lust, ill will, and delusion—and weakened greed, hatred, and delusion. This, Ānanda, is called the fruit of Once-returning. And what, Ānanda, is the fruit of Non-returning? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... unwavering confidence in the Dharma... unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha... Furthermore, he has completely abandoned the five lower fetters. This, Ānanda, is called the fruit of Non-returning. And what, Ānanda, is the fruit of Arhatship? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... unwavering confidence in the Dharma... unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha... Furthermore, he has abandoned the five higher fetters—the conceit of ‘I am,’ restlessness, and ignorance. This, Ānanda, is called the fruit of Arhatship.”

But even so, since an instigation (*pravartanā*) must have a specific person to be instigated as its object, and since that person is required first, and because words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) have the capacity to provide that [person], it is that person alone who is provided by them, not a specific means (*sādhana*). What follows from this? It follows that the qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs to one who possesses desire. Indeed, it is so; yet, there can be no accomplishment of activity (*pravṛtti*) if there is no fruit. And qualification exists for the sake of activity. [Objection: In that case, the instruction (*upadeśa*) would be purposeless. [Reply: It is not purposeless when there is a meaningful object; but if there is none, what else could it be? Alternatively, it is not purposeless because its purpose is the accomplishment of the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavijñāna*). This person, by his very nature, is possessed by passion and the like; being engaged in acquiring objects through visible means, he is intent on attaining them and is partial toward them. He is not capable of either believing or contemplating the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) taught as something in which the manifold of objects has dissolved. However, instructed by the teachings on ritual action (*karman*), having suppressed his natural desires and turned away from spontaneous activity, established in scriptural activity, self-controlled, and with a mind unassailed by desires, he is able to believe and contemplate such a reality of the Self as it is taught. Thus, the injunctions of action serve the purpose of qualifying one for the knowledge of the Self through their visible effects. And in this way, the status of being a scripture (*śāstratva*) arises from instructing the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) or from teaching what is beneficial (*hita*). But if desire were the goal to be accomplished, then because it provides a hand in one's own natural activity—which is pervaded by passion and the like—by showing the means, the word (*śabda*) would transcend the status of being a scripture. For in that case, the person would not be "instructed"; rather, he would be permitted to act according to his own will. Even if the scripture teaches what is beneficial, if it prompts one toward desirable ends that are by nature connected with suffering by showing the means, the word would not be a teacher of the beneficial.

[315,i] But in that case, would not even the injunction regarding knowledge be merely an instruction? No; because knowledge has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) and, by its very nature, is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), like the act of sweeping and so forth. It is with this very point in mind that it was stated: "That which is to be performed should bring happiness; that which is not to be performed should bring suffering," and so on. This is the meaning: since one's own body and so forth are momentary and thus connected with suffering, a sacrifice—which is a means to those—would indeed not be something to be performed if it were itself suffering. However, that which results in happiness and has as its purpose the manifestation of the cessation of the entire proliferation of suffering must be performed. [316,i]

[Objection: But surely, by describing it in this way, the qualification (*adhikāra*) becomes already established. [Response: True. However, no other [qualification] is being defined; it is not a mere admission. Furthermore, how the qualification functions in the sense "one should perform the sacrifice" will be explained later.
[316, ii] To this, it is said:
For it is indeed particulars that are the meanings of words, even when there is an observed conformity of form;
moreover, the cognition of an injunction is not meaningful without the capacity for what is desired.

The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not a mere generality (*sāmānya*), because in common usage only specific instances—such as commanding, requesting, permitting, and instructing—are perceived; furthermore, distinctions such as delusion (*moha*) and the like are understood [from them]. Indeed, there is no instance anywhere where there is a cognition of merely the cause of activity. From a word denoting a generality, there is a cognition of that generality alone only when there is an absence of evidence for a particular; therefore, the meaning of the word is not merely that much. Rather, it is necessarily accompanied by a particular, just as the sense of agency in words like *tṛn* is necessarily accompanied by habitual action (*tācchīlya*), otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the agent even in the absence of its use. Nor are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) non-words, because those not perceived do not effect differentiation, and because there is no other cause for the cognition [of the meaning], and because of the traditional rule: "Since it ends in that, this identical word denotes that. Furthermore, since even "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like are limiting adjuncts, it would follow that the meaning of the word is merely "existence" (*sat*).

[318,i] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of deluded discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of suchness (*tathatā-svabhāva*). Among these, Mahāmati, the self-nature of deluded discrimination refers to the attachment to names, signs, and characteristics based on the various forms of objects, as well as the attachment to the distinctions of one's own and others' schools. The self-nature of dependent origination refers to the manifestation of the various forms of objects through the power of habit-energy (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time, which arises like a dream or a mirage. The self-nature of perfect accomplishment refers to the non-existence of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*) within that dependent nature, which is realized by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) and is free from the duality of grasped and grasper. The self-nature of suchness refers to the state of being as it is, which is the realm of the Tathāgatas, free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and beyond the reach of all philosophical views (*dṛṣṭi*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of self-nature. If one does not understand these four kinds of self-nature, one will fail to realize the stages of a Bodhisattva and will fall into the views of the philosophers. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself in order to transcend the views of the philosophers. Thus it was said: The self-nature of deluded discrimination, The self-nature of dependent origination, The self-nature of perfect accomplishment, And the self-nature of suchness; These are the four kinds of self-nature. (Verse 318)

Even having approached [the subject], it is said: because a general injunction (*sāmānyacodanā*) has a particular as its ultimate referent, it is the particular alone that must be established. And that [particular] may be any one at all, or indeed all; in every case, however, the cognition of the general is meaningful only through the exclusion of the particular. In this regard, neither *preṣaṇā* (command), *adhyeṣaṇā* (request), nor *abhyanujñā* (permission)—which are causes of activity for those who do not depend on desire or capacity but merely follow their own intentions, or for those who depend on them while awaiting their favor—are to be established by [the Veda], which does not originate from human intellect. Nor are delusion (*moha*) and the like [to be established], because they are contrary to cognition. For if these were established, they would not be causes of activity; thus, the comprehension of *pravartanā* (instigation) would be frustrated by the presentation of delusion, and the opposite [of what was intended] would result. Desire (*iṣṭatā*) is not [the cause] with respect to the action, because that would contradict perception. Furthermore, if it did not lead to the understanding of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), it would simply fail to be informative. This is because the cognition of the general would be purposeless if the particular were excluded, resulting in the fallacy of falsity (*mithyātva*). Moreover, that [falsity] is improper in the absence of the two causes [of truth]. As it has been said: "But it is not effective, because it is for that purpose" (*asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt*). The meaning is that the action would be ineffective if it did not find an agent—that is, if there were no qualified person (*adhikārī*). This is because [the Veda] is for that purpose, meaning it aims solely at instigation (*pravartanā*), since the word does not convey that [the action] is a means to pleasure, and human efforts are for the sake of pleasure. However, if it were established that [the action] is a means to pleasure without distinction, then qualification (*adhikāra*) is established. But if all particulars were excluded, the sentence would be ineffective and non-informative, because a general injunction has a non-distinctive object.

[320,i] But was it not said: “The instigation (*pravartanā*) to be manifested by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth is known to be a property of the agent (*prayoktṛdharma*)”? True. However, [the instigation of] a command (*ājñā*) and so forth is not an instruction (*upadeśa*). [Objection: But even an instruction consists in the intention to benefit; thus, it does not transcend being a property of the agent. [320,ii]
This is not sound. For in an instruction (*upadeśa*), the intention (*abhiprāya*) lacks the quality of being a cause for engagement, as is the case with commands (*praiṣa*) and the like. To explain:
in the case of a command and so forth, the power of the action does not depend upon the intention;
rather, in an instruction, one engages after having understood the power of the action.

For one who disregards the capacity of an action regarding both command and request would show no regard for its specific details; this is because it would follow that all words have their meanings already known.

But in that case, the *codanā* would itself be the object of cognition (*prameya*), whereas it is intended to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it is stated that "dharma is an object characterized by the *codanā*. Therefore, the object— which is the cause of activity, which is to be expressed by the word as its own nature, which is to be inferred from the effects of engagement and comprehension, which has action as its domain, which resides in the cognizer, which is self-cognizable, and which is the meaning of the *codanā*— is the *codanā*.

This is incorrect. Since it has been stated that a sentence which is a cause for engagement is a *codanā*—that is, "a *codanā* is a statement that impels one toward action"—let its authority reside in the word itself; what is the use of this superfluous [qualification]? For there is no contradiction with the word in that case. Let its authority be like that of other word-meanings (*padārtha*); the mention of a specific qualification is redundant. And where does its authority lie? If you say in the object (*viṣaya*), no, because that is established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even in the case of a novel (*apūrva*) connection, there is comprehension despite the absence of such [prior] experience, just as in the world. If you say it lies in being a means to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), let it belong to the word alone. If it were an effect of the word, then the application of words would occur for those who have not learned them. It has already been stated that it is illogical for something caused by another factor to be made known by a word. Nor is it [known] through the comprehension of the object, since that is established from the words denoting the object themselves. Nor is it through one's own activity (*pravṛtti*), because that [activity] is absent [prior to the injunction], which would lead to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If the object of activity were [the authority], the word would be useless; if the word were the object, inference would be redundant. If it is argued that there is no redundancy for both because one understands from the word itself after having inferred the connection between the word and its meaning from the activity of another, we say no. From the activity of another, one only perceives the general cause of activity, but because the specific [cause] is not determined, there is no cognition of the [specific] expression of that [cause]. Activity is impossible through the mere comprehension of that [general cause] alone, for not every [general cause] is the cause of activity for everyone. Moreover, [the cause] has a nature that is not caused by anything else. If it is argued that the cause of inference is indeed preceded by the word, since the cognition from the word is preceded by inference, why then is it not simply based on the authority of inference?

[324,i] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are these four? They are: (1) the self-nature of attachment to words; (2) the self-nature of attachment to multiplicity; (3) the self-nature of attachment to discrimination; and (4) the self-nature of the perfected reality. Now, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of attachment to words? It refers to that which is designated by various names and expressions in accordance with the conventional usage of words, such as "elephant," "horse," "ox," "goat," "cloth," "pot," "bowl," and so forth. This is called the self-nature of attachment to words. Next, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of attachment to multiplicity? It refers to the perception of distinct forms and characteristics—such as blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, smooth, coarse, light, heavy, soft, hard, hot, cold, hunger, thirst, and so on—which are apprehended through the sense organs. This is called the self-nature of attachment to multiplicity. Next, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of attachment to discrimination? It refers to the arising of discrimination based upon the aforementioned two types of self-nature, whereby one discriminates between internal and external objects. This is called the self-nature of attachment to discrimination. Next, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the perfected reality? It refers to the realization of the non-existence of the imagined nature within the dependent nature, and the attainment of the state where the dependent nature is seen as being devoid of the imagined nature. This is called the self-nature of the perfected reality. Therefore, Mahāmati, you and other Bodhisattvas should train yourselves in the self-nature of the perfected reality and abandon the self-natures of attachment to words, attachment to multiplicity, and attachment to discrimination.

Furthermore, no cause of activity other than the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is inferred; for that [unseen force] depends on prior establishment, and since activity can be accounted for by visible causes, there is no need for it. Moreover, those specific conditions relied upon by the cognizer must have an objective basis (ālambana) stated, and their status as being established by another means of knowledge must be justified. Even if one accepts a distinct entity [as the cause], if it were eternal, everyone would be entitled to perform [the rite] at all times and in all places, yet such a thing lacks any means of proof, since the cognition of an injunction for someone regarding something arises from the word itself. If it were non-eternal, the word could not be the effect [of that injunction] because of the aforementioned defects. If its production were due to a cause or a desire, it would follow that even one who has already performed the ritual act [would be prompted again]. If it persisted as long as the cause remained, then even for one who has already performed the act, there would be further engagement before the fruits of that action are experienced. Therefore, the injunction is precisely as previously stated. In that regard:
An activity devoted to sacrifice cannot be considered a visible cause [of the result],
since it is presented by the word as being solely intent upon that [sacrifice].

If, indeed, in an operation colored by sacrifice (*yāga*), the sacrifice itself is apprehended as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by virtue of coloring the existence [of the operation], then—since that which is proximate and intended by the word has been stated—the nature of being the cause of the desired result would not reside therein as the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*). This is because that [nature] is not what is intended. In that case, if the injunction is not intended, there might somehow be an engagement with something in the world, whether fruitful or fruitless. As it has been said: "But [the sacrifice] is not the means [to the result], because it exists for the sake of that [result]" (*asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt*). Since human efforts are for the sake of pleasure (*prīti*), if the cause of pleasure does not coincide with the meaning of the injunction, one would not find a means to accomplishment. Now, if it is thus established that the sacrifice rests upon the desired [result] through the power of the injunction, then the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is necessarily concomitant with that [result]. However, if there is no reason to disregard the injunction and the operation of the object is not [intended], then, since the sacrifice is not the desired end, the sacrifice—which is the primary essence—would have no scope within that which is intended by the word. Even if there were scope through another mode, because the injunction has no other scope, it is presented as necessarily concomitant by implication; thus, the sacrifice conforms to the status of being the object (*viṣayatva*) by way of being the instrument.

For one intent on the sacrifice is not intent on the desired object, nor is one intent on the desired object intent on the sacrifice. Thus, first of all, there is a connection with the fruit by virtue of the injunction "one should sacrifice.
And because—first, the status of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as an object is understood in the form of a desire.
Even though heaven is already established, it follows as a result through its connection with that [action].

[327,ii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as existing. He does not perceive form, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive forms, nor does he apprehend them; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive eye-contact, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the realm of form, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the formless realm, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the volitional formations, nor does he apprehend them; he does not perceive consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the conditioned, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the unconditioned, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the past, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the future, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the present, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the world of sentient beings, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the world of vessels, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the world of the gods, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the world of humans, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the world of asuras, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the world of hell-beings, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the world of animals, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the world of hungry ghosts, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the stream-enterer, nor does he apprehend him; he does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the once-returner, nor does he apprehend him; he does not perceive the fruit of once-returning, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the non-returner, nor does he apprehend him; he does not perceive the fruit of non-returning, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the arhat, nor does he apprehend him; he does not perceive the fruit of arhatship, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the pratyekabuddha, nor does he apprehend him; he does not perceive the path of the pratyekabuddha, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend him; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he apprehend it. Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma, that he is called a 'bodhisattva. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives any dharma or apprehends any dharma, he would not be called a 'bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that can be apprehended as a 'bodhisattva,' nor is there any dharma that can be designated as 'bodhisattva. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in this way: 'I shall so purify the perfection of wisdom that I do not perceive any dharma, nor do I apprehend any dharma. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he trains in the perfection of wisdom, and he trains for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. [328,i] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in the perfection of wisdom, train for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in the perfection of wisdom, generates the thought: 'Just as I myself wish to attain nirvāṇa, so too shall I establish all sentient beings in nirvāṇa. Subhūti, although no sentient being is apprehended therein, yet the bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in the perfection of wisdom, does not turn back from the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in the perfection of wisdom, trains for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as supreme perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as supreme perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to as supreme perfect enlightenment, then the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata would not be infinite. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as supreme perfect enlightenment, therefore the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is infinite. Subhūti, if the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata were finite, then the Tathāgata would not be the Teacher of Gods and Men. But because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is infinite, therefore the Tathāgata is the Teacher of Gods and Men. Subhūti, the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is itself infinite, and the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is also infinite. For "whatever one desires, that one undertakes"—thus, desire is the commencement of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force). And since [the object] is to be accomplished by that *bhāvanā*, even though heaven (*svarga*) and the like are already established [as ends], they are connected to the *bhāvanā* in its capacity as its object (*karman*), just as rice and the like are connected to the agent through their status as objects; they are construed with the *bhāvanā* only in their nature as things to be accomplished, and not otherwise. As it has been said: "Because of the connection with each respective object" (*pratyarthaṃ cābhisambandhāt*). The human effort is connected directly toward that which is sought. Therefore, because of its association with seeking, heaven and the like are connected to it as its object; for otherwise, there would be no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). Consequently, in the simple injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), because of the requirement of a result and because heaven cannot be otherwise integrated, it is understood through that connection that the ritual act (*karman*) is the means (*sādhana*) toward heaven. But how can there be a connection of the *bhāvanā* with heaven when it is a qualifier of something else? Or, if such a connection exists, how can it remain a qualifier of another, or how is the compound possible? For there can be no connection with the *bhāvanā* for that which lacks a connection with the [primary] object, or for that which depends on a connection with something else. Furthermore, a compound is not appropriate for that which has become a subordinate member (*guṇabhūta*).
This is not a fault;
for by implication, the word "staff-bearer" enters into a relationship with the qualifier.
And through connection with that [suffix], even when there is a relation with another [word], the compound is not corrupted.

Indeed, heaven (*svarga*) as desired by one seeking heaven is not connected to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) independently of its qualifier; rather, it enters into that connection precisely as something whose primary status is that of a qualifier. Just as in the case of "the staff-bearer recites the directions," the staff-bearer is primarily characterized by his staff, while the staff itself is not intended to be expressed as the primary object of the connection. In this way, the compound is also justified. For if an independent entity were connected with another, a compound would be impossible because of that dependency, since such a connection would be unattainable for an independent thing. However, when there is a connection with another through the mediation of that [qualifier], the unity of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is not obstructed; thus, a compound is logical. Otherwise, every qualifying attribute would result in a compound, because if it did not touch upon the function [of the action], it would be purposeless, and if it did touch upon it, the compound would be impossible due to dependency.

[330,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as being established by way of its own characteristic. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor apprehend any dharma as being established by way of its own characteristic? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature. Since they are empty, they cannot be perceived; since they are empty, they cannot be apprehended. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the thought of awakening? How can he train in the six perfections? How can he enter the path of seeing? How can he enter the path of cultivation? How can he attain the fruit of stream-entry? How can he attain the fruit of once-returning? How can he attain the fruit of non-returning? How can he attain arhatship? How can he attain pratyekabuddhahood? How can he attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty, yet through the power of skillful means, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought of awakening. He trains in the six perfections. He enters the path of seeing. He enters the path of cultivation. He attains the fruit of stream-entry. He attains the fruit of once-returning. He attains the fruit of non-returning. He attains arhatship. He attains pratyekabuddhahood. And he attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening. Subhūti, it is because of emptiness that all these distinctions are established, yet within emptiness there is no distinction whatsoever.”

As for the claim that "when the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*) is the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there can be no co-inherence (*samavāya*) with another thing to be accomplished": in the case of *bhāvanā* (productive activity), its co-inherence [with the end] follows from its very nature, because it has the nature of having the object to be accomplished as its primary element. Even regarding the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), if its status as something to be accomplished were intended primarily through *bhāvanā*, that is set aside by the injunction (*vidhi*). If, however, it is merely the state of being the object of *bhāvanā*, that is common even to other causal factors. For it has been said: "The instrument (*karaṇa*) is everywhere the domain of the agent’s operation. Furthermore, even from the perspective of the word-meanings being substances or qualities, that which is to be produced possesses the status of a means (*sādhana*), because there is no taking up of what is already established. Since sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like, which color (*anurañjayat*) the *bhāvanā* by their very mention (*śruti*), are perceived as its qualifiers, the two-fold nature [of the injunction] is caused by the presence or absence of the *apūrva*. The fact that human effort does not have the sacrifice as its direct object is not contradictory even in the case of heaven; it is like the axe having the tree as its object when the tree is to be cut. Nor is the sacrifice non-activity (*avyāpāra*), since it is understood from the word itself. Moreover, we accept that even the arising of cognitions and lamps is an activity. Nor is heaven eternally non-existent such that it would be impossible to attain; if it is argued that this is due to ignorance of the means, then for that very reason it is made known [by the Veda]. Nor does this entail the consequence that [the sacrifice] must necessarily be performed, because the injunction (*vidhi*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the fruit-portion and a summary of the instrumental portion, as in the case of "He offers with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*). And since the inclination toward the fruit is directed toward the sacrifice as its object, the word is the cause [of that inclination], and thus the sacrifice is enjoined. For the person’s inclination toward the action is not one thing, and the inclination toward the instrument another. One who is inclined toward the instrument becomes inclined toward the fruit; one who is being impelled toward the action is impelled toward the instrument. Thus, because the meaning is understood in this way, there is no futility, nor is there any other purpose [for the injunction] than "one desiring heaven should perform the sacrifice. If the word were fixed solely on the sacrifice, then because of its co-inherence [with the fruit], it would lack authority, resulting in the abandonment of what is heard and the assumption of what is unheard. Nor is the visible purpose—the realization of the Self—[the goal], because through rituals that exhaust desires, the mind becomes subdued; and for one whose mind is not agitated by desires, the reality of the Self is easily realized. If rituals indeed exhaust desires and one who has achieved his ends through them requires no further purpose, then the injunction of ritual is devoted solely to that [exhaustion of desire]; thus there is no evidence for it being devoted to anything else. Nor is it non-scriptural (*aśāstra*), because it expresses what is beneficial (*śreyaḥ*). Benefit consists of the form of pleasure (*prīti*), and pleasure is individually experienced within desires. Nor is enjoyment the exhaustion [of desire], for there is no satiety in desires. If it is argued that it is by the cessation of other activities, then even there, if the desirer should accomplish [his goal] by sacrifice and not by some other means, what is the difference? If the mind is in the state of desiring, how can there be a cessation of desire in an activity belonging to that side? Furthermore, how can there be a cessation of other options in an injunction where nothing was previously established? If it is argued that the desirer should perform the sacrifice and not the desire, two meanings are difficult to obtain without distinction—one expressed directly (*śrauta*) and one indicated (*lākṣaṇika*). If the injunction is devoted to the sacrifice, there is no prohibition of desire; if it is devoted to the prohibition of desire, there is no injunction of the sacrifice. The cessation of desire would follow only by implication (*arthāt*), because both cannot co-exist. Moreover, if all activities aimed at visible ends are opposed by the injunction of ritual, they would become useless, since their purpose is achievable through visible means. And since the enjoyment of results is natural, the meaning of the Veda would effectively be the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*) adopted under a pretext. Therefore, this is a great burden: that the injunctions of ritual ascend to the qualification for self-knowledge only through visible means. The teaching of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-anuśāsana*) is the function of scripture; thus, even the injunction of knowledge is merely the teaching of the person to be enjoined, and therefore the realization of the Self does not arise from it. If it is argued that it arises from the very nature of knowledge, then the injunction is futile. If it is argued that it is like the act of threshing (*avahanti*), no; for that is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). There is no restriction to a specific type of knowledge, because it is not established even as an alternative (*pakṣe*). And since it is possible through superimposition (*samāropa*), there is no determination of reality (*tattvapariccheda*). Therefore, when the meaning of the verbal root is not a means, there is no establishment of the modification (*vikāra*). And it has been stated that its status as a means is the injunction.
Thus ends the *Vidhiviveka*, composed by the venerable Great Preceptor Maṇḍanamiśra.
